speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house I should like to report in general on the visit which I made last Friday and Saturday to Washington at the invitation of President Eisenhower. As I pointed out on my arrival there, this was not a formal visit; it was the kind of call which one makes on a close neighbour with whom one is on friendly terms and with whom one is in the habit of talking over matters of mutual interest.
I particularly point out the warmth of the welcome extended to me because I represented Canada, both by the President himself, his secretary of state and all the officials and members of the public with whom I came in contact. We are bound to have differences between our countries, as friends and neighbours will, but beneath the surface of whatever intermittent strains may arise in our relationship there is a vein of continued understanding and good will that springs not only from our heritage but also from the common sense of the importance of being united in safeguarding common values.
I am going to refer to one or two of the matters which were discussed, although I know the house will not expect me to go into any detail on the substance of those talks. We found ourselves in agreement with regard to the circumstances which led to the summit failure and also the position which the western nations should now adopt individually and within the NATO alliance in their relations with the Soviet union. The need is to establish and preserve an equilibrium between the maintenance of defensive preparedness on the one hand and on the other a continued readiness to retain existing contacts with the Soviet world and extend those contacts on the basis of mutual agreement whenever the opportunity arises.
I discussed with the President matters connected with the future policies in NATO. I expressed the view that the time had come for the NATO nations to re-examine the
capacity of that alliance to deal with the problems which lie ahead. Hon. members will recall that at the ministerial meeting of NATO last December the United States secretary of state proposed that a study be made of long range planning for the 1960's. My view, which I expressed to the President, was that recent international happenings had increased the urgency of undertaking this study.
The United States is already engaged in preliminary work along these lines. My view was that after that study had been fully proceeded with the NATO governments should give early and serious attention to the holding of a meeting at heads of government level in order that those who have the responsibilities of leadership may join in a collective effort to establish and sketch new lines of endeavour for NATO in the years ahead. All of us are fully conscious of the importance of thorough preliminary consultation, for unless we achieve the free interflow of ideas and suggestions in the future we cannot take advantage of the opportunity to open up new and secure paths of progress for the alliance.
I further stated that should it be agreed that a heads of government meeting of NATO should take place, Canada would be prepared to extend invitations to the NATO leaders to hold that meeting in Canada.
I discussed with the President the proposal which he put forward first in 1955, and to which he referred in recent public statements, that consideration should be given to a system of aerial inspection as a means of removing the threat of surprise attack. In that connection he pointed out the views expressed by the Leader of the Opposition in support of action in that direction. The President confirmed that study was being given to the open skies proposal. I said that such a proposal, if and when advanced in the United Nations, should have co-sponsors and that Canada would join in sponsoring an appropriate resolution in that regard.
Other subjects were generally of an international nature, the outlook for progress on disarmament and the ending of nuclear weapons tests. There was agreement on the importance of pursuing negotiations on these matters which would serve at the moment as important and continuing points of contact with the Soviet government. Information on the most recent Soviet disarmament plans as enunciated by Mr. Khrushchev was not

Prime Minister's Visit to Washington available in a comprehensive form and it was therefore not possible to discuss this development in any detail. However, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in the house last Friday, although the Soviet proposals are heavily weighted in propaganda aspects the western nations should demonstrate a readiness to examine them with serious intent, and the agency for that consideration exists in the 10-nation committee on disarmament which will resume its deliberations tomorrow in Geneva.
As for the bilateral relations between United States and Canada, various aspects of policies affecting the two countries jointly were discussed, including continental defence and problems in the trade and economic fields. We spoke frankly about the concern that Canadians feel over recent United States wheat surplus disposal policies which could damage Canadian wheat export markets, particularly in Latin America and Africa. However, I think I can sum up the general feeling and the attitude that was shown during these discussions by reading the words of the communique and drawing particular attention to those in the concluding paragraph:
The Prime Minister and the President reviewed the course of relations between their countries during recent years and noted with pleasure the extent to which the problems arising in such relations have yielded to the process of friendly and continuing consultation. They considered that satisfactory means of carrying on such consultations have been established in personal exchanges as well as by regular diplomatic arrangements and the various joint committees that have been created. They expressed their belief that there has been established between the two countries-
I know the house will concur in this.
-a model for the relationship between neighbours.
Again I repeat, sir, that the unusual warmth of the welcome and the expressions not only of friendship but of a desire to cooperate in every way so as not to cause harm one to the other were most apparent, and I must publicly express my thanks and appreciation for everything that was done on the part of our great neighbour to show its feelings toward our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members of the house will have listened with interest to the Prime Minister's report and I am sure all were happy that it was possible for him to continue a practice which has now extended over many years and to take advantage of the opportunity to visit Washington and confer with the President of the United States; particularly at this rather difficult time in the history of relations between the east and west and indeed a time of some difficulty in regard to relations inside 
the coalition. By "difficulty" I mean it is a time of stocktaking and re-examination, not so much of the purposes and principles of the coalition, because there has been no doubt about that, but as to how we can best achieve the objective we have set for ourselves within the group.
I am sure the Prime Minister had the kind-it is obvious from what we have heard-of warm and friendly reception that Canadian leaders always get when they go to Washington, even though they go down there on occasion to talk very frankly to our friends and neighbours.
I am sure this meeting, like others before it, was useful as well as pleasant. In his statement the Prime Minister added something to a communique which was very short and general in character, and we are glad to get the information he has given us. We read that communique, Mr. Speaker, along with the statements that appeared in the press on the meeting in question. I note, for instance, that both the President and the Prime Minister-and I certainly have no quarrel with this-emphasized that the tactics pursued by the leader of the Soviet union in recent days, tactics at least of verbal aggression, have had the result that such tactics always have and which they do not seem to understand on the other side of the iron curtain, of bringing members of the coalition closer together rather than splitting them apart.
While that is true, Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that this is not a satisfactory or a very certain basis of unity. To have our unity strengthened in that negative way, on that shock-treatment basis, if you like, is not good enough. Therefore, recent developments have shown not only the necessity of coming closer together in the face of a common danger but, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, they have shown also the insufficiency and inadequacy of present methods of consultation inside the alliance. And by "consultation" I do not mean the giving of information after decisions have been taken, but consultation on every aspect of policy inside the alliance before decisions are taken.
I am glad the Prime Minister has once again emphasized the necessity of this, but we will never get it merely by talking about it. Indeed, we have been talking about it now for a good many years; so while I welcome this examination of the policy of NATO in the 1960's, which the Prime Minister has referred to this morning, I doubt whether any further examination of the need of consultation and unity inside the alliance will add very much to the studies we have already made in NATO in the past on that subject.

If it were possible tor NATO governments to carry out recommendations which have already been made about consultations and cooperation, the organization would be far more effective than it is at present. While a NATO summit meeting-if I may refer to it in those terms-may be a helpful thing to have, I could hope that in the case of that summit meeting the work will have been done before the meeting is held, and that NATO will be able to implement some of the recommendations already made. All that is required is for the governments in NATO to carry out the recommendations made; to make NATO more effective not only in defence but in nonmilitary matters. In so far as defence is concerned, the time has come to have another look at the possibility of having a really collective system which would include North America as a NATO sector of defence. I say that because if we have learned anything from the events of the last month surely it is that defence is not divisible, and that we cannot talk about western European NATO defence and ignore the North American sector of that defence.
One of the things that is mentioned in the communique, but just mentioned, is the subject of the defence relationship between the two countries. There is greater elaboration of that point in some of the press comment on the conference. Indeed, in the New York Times of yesterday there was a headline to the effect that the Canadian Prime Minister gets assurance by the United States that the President has pledged his backing and presumably the backing of the United States on defence planning and the Bomarc missile program. If it had been possible for the Prime Minister to give it we would have welcomed some information on that score. Where do we stand now on these matters of defence?
The communique has one very important reference to this matter which perhaps I might read. It is in these words:
Particular attention was paid to the importance of achieving, with effective international control, an end to nuclear testing and progress toward general disarmament.
That is a very important statement, Mr. Speaker, that attention has been paid particularly to the importance of achieving an end to nuclear testing, with effective international control. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has told us more than once in the house that the policy of the government in that regard is an end of nuclear testing, period. When I have asked him in the house whether that meant an end of nuclear testing with controls he has repeated that he meant an end of testing, period. The possible ambiguity and doubt between that statement 79951-0-286

I am glad some discussion took place about disarmament and the United Nations. Once again the head of the Soviet government has made what seems to be one of those sensational proposals that make it look as if we have something new before us. The disarmament committee is going to meet tomorrow, and I hope there will be no delay in Geneva in taking him up on this at once and finding out what, if anything, is behind it.
The Prime Minister mentioned also the desirability of pressing ahead with the open skies proposal. I cannot think of anything much more important than that in the light of what has happened in the last month. Perhaps I might just recall at this time, because the Prime Minister mentioned Canada's connection with this matter, that back in 1955 the Canadian representative to the disarmament committee of that day, the hon. member for Essex East, put before that group this proposal for open skies. At that time there was not too much support for the Canadian initiative. Perhaps the time has now come to take this up again as a Canadian proposal at the United Nations and to associate with Canada in this regard-the Prime Minister mentioned the desirability of this- a group of middle powers who can press ahead with this as a middle power proposition, in view of the fact that the great powers are so suspicious of each other in connection with implementing such a proposal. There might be greater likelihood of something resulting from a group of middle powers taking the initiative and following it through, and taking the responsibility under the United Nations for implementing it without the participation of the great powers.
These and other things should be pressed, of course, with great vigour at this particular time, because public opinion is surely alert now to the necessity of doing something because of the kind of shock treatment it has received. Shocks will wear off, however, and if we do not take advantage of this situation we will be tempted to lapse back into the kind of situation we have been in so often, of assuming that because we get some kind words again, following bad words, everything is going to be all right.
The Prime Minister mentioned that economic matters were considered in Washington. I certainly hope they were. I agree with the Prime Minister that compared with relations between most other neighbouring countries those between Canada and the United States are a model. Nevertheless it is a model which can be improved upon.

Prime Minister's Visit to Washington One way in which it can be improved is in the field of trading and economic relationships so that those relationships will include the kind of co-operation which we are expected to give in defence itself. It has so often been said in the house by members on both sides that if we are to co-operate in defence we must co-operate in defence production. Perhaps the Prime Minister had the opportunity in Washington-I do not know whether he did-of reminding the President that one part of defence production is defence materials, and we are not going to have the kind of co-operation which we should have if we can be turned on and off as a source of defence materials to meet the exigencies of economic and political situations in the United States.
So, Mr. Speaker, we welcome the Prime Minister's talks in Washington and we hope they will yield concrete results. But surely the time has come, especially in the United Nations and in NATO, when all the fine talk of the last 10 years must be converted, in the light of the dangers and difficulties of the last month, into some kind of concrete action.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this group appreciate the Prime Minister's moderation, tenor and tone in making his report to the house as a result of his visit with President Eisenhower. I am going to be quite brief, but I do wish to emphasize this on behalf of this group. The point of view of this group at the present time is in general that this is not a time for political pyrotechnics or recriminations or threats from any source. This is a time for the calm presentation of constructive views and action. From our point of view, this is the time for Canada to give constructive, forceful and co-operative leadership to the middle and smaller powers in the promotion of an atmosphere that will dissipate the apprehensions of the world at this time.
We urge the government to seize with both hands this opportunity to render a tremendous service to mankind. We also believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) has the capacity, the ability and the point of view that will enable him to give constructive and effective leadership at this time.

The minister, as I recall it, has stated that the intention is not to persecute but to establish what are the facts and then do our best to clear up and regularize the situation; in which process she hopes to have-and I am sure will have-the co-operation of the Chinese community itself.
With regard to questions earlier asked by the hon. member as to whether I had representations from the Chinese benevolent association of Vancouver, may I say that I have now received a letter dated June 3 containing two sets of resolutions from the Chinese benevolent association in Vancouver, the letter having been received by me this morning, June 6.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Acting Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SAN FRANCISCO, CAL.-REQUEST FOR OPENING OF TEMPORARY TOURIST CENTRE
speechtext:
On
Friday last the hon. member for Nipissing asked this question:
In view of the government's refusal to establish a tourist information centre in San Francisco this year on a regular basis, will the government now consider the opening of such a centre on a trial basis, with the appropriate promotion, for this summer season?


I think I cannot do better than refer to the reply given by the minister of northern affairs on May 4 to a question asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). At that time the minister said there had been a significant increase in the amount of money available to the Canadian government travel bureau for the current fiscal year. In working out priorities for getting the most value from the dollars spent, it was decided to lay the emphasis this year on increased direct advertising in the United States and on information material for distribution. As a result, funds were just not available to establish an office in San Francisco at this time.
I think it will be evident to the hon. member that the same consideration would apply to the opening of a tourist information centre on a trial basis for this summer season. To do so would require a reduction in the advertising, which would be most undesirable. I would remind the hon. member, too, that a venture of this kind requires careful advance planning, even though it is experimental, and it is much too late in the season to put out the promotion that would be necessary to make the work of such a centre most effective.
I should add that the Canadian consulates in San Francisco, Los Angeles and other centres will continue to deal with travel inquiries on behalf of the Canadian government travel bureau. I can assure the hon. member that the desirability of opening additional travel offices in the United States, as well as the question of travel promotion in Europe, about which the hon. member inquired recently, is continuing to receive the closest attention of the government.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, June 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fulton for the second reading of Bill No. C-58, to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned on Wednesday last I was seeking to deal with the principle set out in clause 17 (4) of the bill, a wholly new principle, as I was endeavouring to show. I had just started to deal with that phase of the matter, and I had quoted the clause which in my submission had provided a new alternative method of proceeding in these cases, a proceeding by way of information rather than by way of prosecution.
The significant word is "or", making it quite clear that there are alternative methods of proceeding. Formerly the proceeding for a mandatory or prohibitory order had been merely an ancillary or additional method to the penalties provided under the criminal prosecution. This clause now introduces an alternative to the criminal prosecution, and I had just started to point out the objections to that course of proceeding.
The word "information" is of course used in proceedings commenced by the crown whether by way of criminal prosecution or, as in the case of the exchequer court, proceedings by way of civil action. It will be found in rule 3 of the exchequer court rules that all suits on behalf of Her Majesty in the right of Canada are, unless otherwise provided by statute of the parliament of Canada, to be instituted by information, and so on.
The point I was making was that since the word "prosecution" obviously refers to criminal prosecution and the word "information" used in the clause is an alternative to criminal prosecution, the word "information" must denote the commencement of civil proceedings by the crown. Since the whole basis of the jurisdiction of this parliament under former anti-combines legislation is that it is criminal law-the offence is made a crime-this materially weakens, and indeed it could be argued may even destroy, the whole anti-combines legislation if I am right in my submission that this clause gives a new alternative method which is a wholly civil method of proceeding as an alternative to criminal proceedings.
There are other objections to this new principle. One objection is the taking of an
Combines Investigation Act arbitrary power by the Minister of Justice; and while the cabinet must speak collectively, and I cannot ask any one cabinet minister how the principle which gave the Minister of Justice this arbitrary power was dealt with, I do hope the Prime Minister will deal with that point before this debate concludes, because of the attacks which have been made by the present government in past years on anything which they interpreted as giving arbitrary power to a minister. Yet here we are presented with legislation in which the minister seeks to determine whether civil or criminal proceedings will be taken in the event of a breach of the provisions. Moreover, he seeks to exercise that discretion not in accordance with any criteria set out in the act of parliament, but merely in accordance with his own opinions.
This is a wholly offensive method of proceeding. I would hope that our laws would be determined by the parliament of Canada, and that we have not reached the stage of giving a minister of justice the right to substitute his own opinions for those of the parliament of Canada in determining the law.
If the clause is objectionable on those two grounds, it is also objectionable on a third. It creates the possibility of favouritism being shown by the Minister of Justice, and the hon. gentleman surely does not wish that those who follow him in his office should be confronted with the necessity of making a decision as to whether proceedings to be commenced against a company which is in breach of this act shall be on the basis of criminal or civil law.
What are the criteria to be? Is it companies who have presidents who have no hair at all who are to be dealt with under civil law? Is it men who have red hair who are to be taken to the criminal courts and not to the civil courts? The whole of the solution proposed to us amounts to an absurdity, yet we are being asked to enact it as legislation. It is wholly wrong, and those who follow the present minister in office and exercise this discretion will always be suspected of showing favouritism on one ground or another.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask a question?

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have only 20 minutes in which to put forward my argument. I will be glad to answer the hon. gentleman's question at the conclusion of what I have to say, but I am trying to cover two or three points.
There is one other objection to this clause. It will be noted that the discretion allowed to the minister may also be exercised by the attorneys general of the provinces. There are ten different provinces. It is by no means difficult to imagine a situation where in one of
4538	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act these provinces every company in breach of the act would be proceeded against by way of civil proceedings, while in another part of the country they would all be proceeded against by way of criminal prosecution.
Surely, in these circumstances, the parliament of Canada cannot be asked to set up legislation which, in effect, depends on the manner in which its provisions are carried out by the provincial attorneys general. Surely we are not to be left in the position where in one province, which may take a very unkind view of anti-combines legislation, there would be no prosecutions under the Criminal Code but merely civil proceedings, while in another province, where a different view might be taken, all the prosecutions would be under the provisions of the criminal law. I can even envisage a situation where one province might decide that it wished to attract within its jurisdiction many of the companies which were carrying on these practices, intending to be very friendly toward them. So the legislation is bad from that point of view.
The clause, as I see it, is wholly offensive. It is directly contrary to the minister's declaration that he was adopting and preserving the principles of anti-combines legislation as they exist. It is further objectionable on the ground that it gives arbitrary power to the minister. It is the key clause in the bill now before us; it is wholly bad, and it should be rejected.
I wish to turn to another subject in the few minutes remaining to me. I propose to deal with that part of the bill which has to do with retail price maintenance, or the old section 34 of the act. That is to be found in clause 14 of the bill, and in my respectful submission clause 14 again introduces a wholly new principle. The principle in the legislation as it exists is that resale price maintenance is illegal. Section 34-and I will read only a few phrases of it-provides:
No dealer shall directly or indirectly by agreement, threat, promise or any other means whatsoever, require or induce or attempt to require or induce any other person to resell an article or commodity
(a)	at a price specified by the dealer or established by agreement,
(b)	at a price not less than a minimum price specified by the dealer or established by agreement.
And so on.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
On a
point of order, it seems to me that on the second reading of the bill it would be out of order to read individual clauses. We will no doubt be repeating all this when we come to a clause by clause discussion in committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext: The principle which the hon. member states is quite acceptable and well established, but its application is not quite so simple. Here we have a bill which makes three or four main changes, and I do not altogether see how an hon. member can discuss any of the three or four principal amendments without reference in some detail. I must say that the minister, in presenting his argument, avoided any reading of the various sections or even reference to them by number. I hope that as far as possible hon. members will reserve the detailed discussion until we reach the committee stage.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I accept the point raised by the hon. member. But there are three principles included in this bill, as I read it; they are contained in three particular sections, and I have no way of referring to them other than by way of the clauses in which they are contained. I have no intention of discussing the clauses as such; I am concerned only with the argument as to principle.
This third principle is the one concerning resale price maintenance. The minister stated that he was maintaining the principle of existing legislation; yet in clause 14, as I shall seek to show, he goes a long way, if not the whole of the way, toward totally removing the effectiveness of the present provisions concerning resale price maintenance. I wish to refer to some remarks which I mentioned at the opening of my part in this debate, namely the remarks made by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) as they appear at page 4432 of Hansard. I notice the hon. member is not here, and I think I should quote him precisely so there may be no confusion. Incidentally, I wish also to refer to remarks made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). I took the precaution of asking the government whip to ask the hon. member to be here, since I intended to refer to what he had said. In any event, the hon. member for Davenport, as appears on page 4432, presented for the consideration of the house a pamphlet which had been put out by the retail businessmen's association. I shall quote only part of the pamphlet. I hope that hon. members who are following the subject will have taken note of the hon. member's remarks, because I do not want to take them out of context. The pamphlet read in part:
A whopping 94 per cent of retailers who replied to this paper's queries on pricing said they favour a return to manufacturer-enforced retail prices, and 92 per cent agreed the present free for all price system is definitely harmful to business.

Then further down the hon. member in his own words went on to state:
I think that should definitely establish that there is a call, a requirement, by small businessmen for some change; and the change that is being suggested by the government is to try to meet that need.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka took part in the debate and at page 4422 of Hansard of June 1 he referred to a letter dated April 28, 1960 and quoted from that letter the part relating to resale price maintenance. The hon. gentleman went on to say:
I was pointing out that what these people ask is exactly what is included in this bill.
I remarked earlier that I was very happy to see government members take part in this debate, because I think the participation of these two hon. members shows the importance of government members and opposition members debating a subject of this magnitude. These two hon. members have disclosed what the legislation is intended to do, depending on how you interpret their words. If I were to interpret them exactly as they sound the words of one hon. member at least could be taken to mean that the bill reintroduces resale price maintenance. I do not think he intended to go that far, although his words go that far. In any event that is exactly what clause 14 does.
I would point out that with all the talk there has been about loss leader selling, and so on, there is nothing in this bill that attempts to make loss leader selling illegal or anything of that sort. There is provided by a most indirect and devious route a defence to a man charged with a breach of the existing anti-combines legislation. A man charged on the ground that he is really enforcing resale price maintenance on his retailers can now avail himself of these defences set out in clause 14. This indirect method of doing it has the effect of destroying the legislation as it presently exists. It is quite interesting that the two government members who took part in the debate discussed certain things they thought were offensive, but they quoted excerpts from pamphlets submitted to parliament by private organizations that were attacking the legislation on resale price maintenance and were urging the restoration of that practice. That is what they said the legislation did.
The minister dealt with certain other related subjects and said he had provided in the bill for the subject matter he was discussing, if I interpret him correctly, but the bill does not do anything of the sort. The bill provides certain additional defences to charges of breaches of the existing legislation. Now, if the minister had intended only to deal
Combines Investigation Act with certain of these other matters discussed he would, I respectfully submit, have dealt with the matter directly by providing for it in the legislation instead of providing these defences that undermine the whole legislation on this point.
There are some other objectionable principles introduced here. Instead of delineation of the offences, we have merely done it by indirection through providing defences to persons accused of another matter altogether; but we have also done something else. We have really substituted for our traditional method of delineating these offences by parliament and having the courts administer the law, a new method which puts the supplier or wholesaler in a curious position because he is now to be the policeman for his actions. He is to be the court. I ask hon. members who are interested in the subject to consider the significance of the latter part of subclause 5 of clause 14, which states:
Where, in a prosecution under this section, it is proved that the person charged refused or counselled the refusal to sell or supply an article to any other person, no inference unfavourable to the person charged shall be drawn from such evidence if he satisfies the court that he and anyone upon whose report he depended had reasonable cause to believe and did believe-
Then follows a certain list of things. In other words, we are to set up some kind of private policing arrangement run by the supplier whereby, let us say, if a competitive retailer wants to injure his competitors he can get the supplier-and he may be sincere in believing there were breaches of the things enumerated-to say there was a breach. If the supplier believes that he has a good defence to the charge of maintaining prices that we have created by our legislation, he may use that defence. Surely that is an extraordinary way of attacking the whole problem. Surely that is offensive to parliament and a wrong method of dealing with the matter.
I do not want to go into a more technical discussion of the clauses, but I would point out that as I see the bill there are three new main principles introduced. If I am right in interpreting them they all either materially weaken the anti-combines legislation or possibly even wipe it out.
One of the principles is to be found in the provision providing for a setting out of the type of combines that are legal. That is entirely objectionable on two grounds. One, it gives the corporation which have a mind to create combines that are illegal under the act a golden opportunity to get together to further that object under the guise of dealing with these legal combines. The other objection is that it gives the vast majority of corporations which are anxious not to be in that position

Combines Investigation Act and to observe the law carefully no opportunity to be sure whether they are doing so, because there is no provision for dealing with these combines or agreements that are made legal, no registration or anything like that which would enable the director to look at them and accept them if they are not offensive and to police the combines.
There are other objections as well to the new principles introduced. There is, of course, no protection at all for the consumer in the new principle introduced in that clause. Then there is also the clause I have spoken about today, subclause 4 of clause 17. That is a wholly new principle. This legislation was always regarded as within the competence of parliament because it was criminal legislation, and was always supported by penal provisions after criminal prosecution although, it is true, with certain ancillary rights to issue a mandatory order as ancillary to the criminal prosecution.
That whole principle is now violated. A new principle is introduced; that is, there can be an alternative, either criminal prosecution or proceeding by way of information and merely an application for a mandatory order, a prohibitory order, as the case may be. Therefore that principle as a new principle is wholly offensive. Then there is an offshoot of that, the arbitrary power of the minister and the offensive principle of giving the attorney general in each province the right to determine what procedure shall be used, civil or criminal, in these cases.
Then there is this new principle on the subject of resale price maintenance, which effectively destroys the legislation against retail price maintenance which gave the retailers an opportunity to compete and which was, as I think time has shown and certainly as the subsequent investigations have shown, such that there has not been any cause to complain about it, and it certainly has been a great boon to the consumers of this country.
As I see this legislation, Mr. Speaker, it is wholly objectionable because it is wrong in principle. The other point is that it introduces principles-and there are three of them

which are harmful. It is harmful, of course, to the whole approach we have had in this country of trying to control combines which are set up to exploit the public. It is wholly harmful to the interests of consumers, and curiously enough it is wholly harmful to the interests of the retailers, the small businessmen about whom so much was said, and it surely cannot be very satisfactory to the corporations which are seeking to avoid creating any offence and carry on business in the proper way.


For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, as far as I am concerned the legislation should be opposed and destroyed, if possible, before it becomes the law of this country. I do hope that the minister, who is not limited as to time in debate as I am, will seek to deal with the points I have raised.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) had a question, and I cut him off because I did not want to take up the time at that point.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the house for any great length of time, but a few things have been said, particularly by hon. members on the opposition benches, that I feel I must comment on. In my riding I have a great many small businesses and it is my personal opinion that this legislation will help them to a very great extent.
I have read most of the speeches made so far in this debate, and I was particularly interested in those which dealt with the historical aspects of combines or anti-combines legislation. The Minister of Justice gave us a very full and detailed historical dissertation on this subject and the Leader of the Opposition did likewise. I would say that I much prefer the Minister of Justice as a history professor, in view of the two speeches that were given in the house.
The hon. member for Gatineau also dealt at length with the historical aspects. In particular he pointed out that as a result of his efforts in the house there was an investigation into the pulpwood industry which did a great deal of good for people in his constituency. As I understand it, there was a prosecution and his constituents benefited from that prosecution.
But it is interesting to note that a very important chapter was left out by both the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Gatineau. This important chapter centres around the ministers of the crown who were on the treasury benches not so long ago, particularly the last minister of justice, Hon. Mr. Garson. It also centres around a flour case. I believe there was a great deal of debate in the house on that point, and I understand the director of the combines branch resigned. But the hon. member for Gatineau and the Leader of the Opposition chose to leave this important chapter out of the history of the combines legislation. I would certainly hope that at some future date we who were not here at that time can be brought up to date on just exactly what took place.

1 note also that the bible of the Liberal party has not been quoted in this debate. I refer in particular to an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of May 18 of this year. I am not surprised that this editorial has not been quoted. Indeed, it is one of the vilest editorials I have ever read, and I believe it was written from a completely prejudiced point of view and was not based very much on facts. There is one particular point in this editorial which I hope the Minister of Justice will deal with when he concludes the debate. I think it is an extremely serious charge, and I certainly hope that he will deal at length with this sentence which appears in the editorial:
The Minister of Justice is given authority to suppress an investigation without being answerable to parliament.
I think this is a very serious charge for any responsible newspaper in this country to make.
The Liberal party and the C.C.F. party in the house have said that they are absolutely and completely opposed to this legislation; yet when one reads the speeches that have been made one finds that they are in favour of the consumer, of small business and of big business. They do not realize that this legislation is intended to benefit not only the consumer, to help not only small business but is not intended in any way-nor do I think it will-to criticize, to ridicule or to do anything else to big business. It will in no way persecute it.
I should like to quote some of the reactions to this legislation which have come from those people who are connected and concerned with small business. In particular I should like to quote a telegram which was sent from Ottawa to Mr. E. E. Bimm at Eganville. This is a retail merchants' association dispatch from Ottawa, dated May 7 of this year, and it reads as follows:
R.M.A. dispatch from Ottawa. New measures designed to protect small businessmen introduced in commons today. Legislation retains proposed curbs against misleading price advertising and loss leader selling. The major new provision is a ban against discriminatory promotional allowances and will demand that in every case where a promotional allowance is awarded to one store the same allowance in proportion to purchase must be made to other stores. This would be of immediate benefit to independents. The main provision respecting trade practices are amendments to section 34 and section 412 Criminal Code. It is a momentous week for R.M.A.
This is just one telegram in response to this legislation. It is significant to note that when the bill was introduced last year there was the same response from people connected with small business interests. I refer to a telegram directed to the director of investigation and research of the combines branch,
Combines Investigation Act Mr. T. D. MacDonald, from the retail merchants' association of Manitoba. The telegram reads:
Re your letter June 22 I have not received letter May 19. Please forward copy. A million thanks to you and your department for work on new proposed legislation.
We could go through others that were presented. Another such telegram is from J. D. Bastable, president of the Manitoba division of the retail merchants' association, addressed to the Minister of Justice. It is dated June 12, 1959 and reads as follows:
Congratulations and a sincere thank you on behalf of the retailers of Manitoba on your proposed loss leader selling and false advertising legislation.
This in part indicates the reaction of the small business people in our country, and I want to direct my remarks particularly to that segment of our economy. If you look at the briefs that have been presented to the government over the years by the Canadian wholesale council, the retail merchants' association, the tobacco distributors and other segments concerned in the small business operations of the country, you will appreciate the number of people employed by small businesses, the amount of business they do and the service they give to their communities, and you will realize that they have made an exhaustive study of this matter and that every one of their briefs advocates that something must be done with regard to unfair discounts and loss leader selling.
My own experience with small business is a personal one. I was born and raised in a country store, and I know some of the problems that small stores have in meeting the prices of the larger chain stores. I have been in touch with every drug store in my constituency and have called on a great many of the corner grocery stores, and have found that fewer people are employed in these stores as pharmacists, clerks and delivery boys than in 1955, for instance. Their volume of business is greater today than in 1955, but the income tax they pay is lower and the number of people they hire is less simply because they are meeting prices and competing in a field where substantial discounts are given to the larger stores; therefore the prices they pay for their products are often higher than the prices at which other stores are selling them. Not only that, but they are competing against loss leaders as well as big discounts.
I do not believe that any government should interfere to any great extent with commercial operations, but if the world of business will not formulate a code of ethics which will be fair to all then the government must intervene and pass legislation so that the small man

Combines Investigation Act who is at a disadvantage will receive some protection. Would it not be wonderful in this day and age to be able to go into a store and buy a small tube of toothpaste at a regular price? No such thing exists today. The smallest tube of toothpaste you can get is the large size, and it is always sold at a discount. These are practices in our economy that are unfair. They are unfair to the small man, the corner grocer, the family unit that must give credit in order to survive and which thereby provide a service to the community that the larger stores will not give. They provide a delivery service and they are open at all hours of the night.
The plea of the small businessman must be heard, and in my estimation it has been heard in this legislation. I feel that by this legislation the consumer will benefit, the small businessman will be able to survive and big business will not be persecuted in any way. I had hoped that the bill would have been referred to the committee on banking and commerce before now, because in my view representations should be made with respect to the various clauses of the bill by those persons in our country who are concerned with this matter and who have given it exhaustive study.
I am very disappointed at the attitude of both the official opposition and the C.C.F. party. I am extremely disappointed, because while they have taken the attitude that they are all in favour of small business they have not offered very much in the way of constructive ideas. Their remarks have bordered upon repetition and have been the same thing over and over again. They are in favour of small business but against the bill. I should like to see them sit down, study the bill and let it go to the committee where representations can be made. In the end I think they will find that the bill is intended to give and will give the small businessman of this country something he has been advocating for a long time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to make a few remarks on this anaemic legislative child which the Minister of Justice has presented to the house for baptism. Before


doing so, if I correctly heard the hon. member who has just taken his seat he said that he was born in a country store. This is the first time I have ever heard of a Conservative being born in a country store. I was born in a country bed. However, I thought what he said was very interesting.
I did not have the opportunity to be here last Monday when the Minister of Justice presented the bill to the house, because I was attending the Legion convention in Windsor at the request of a number of delegates of the British Columbia section of the Canadian Legion. However, since returning I have read the minister's speech very carefully. I give him credit for very careful preparation, but in reading his speech I got the impression that while he was presenting this bill to the house and therefore placing it before the jury of the country, he was something like a socialist addressing a Progressive Conservative convention in that he was treading warily.
In dealing with this legislation may I point out that the desire to combine to the advantage of the few and the disadvantage of the many represents, of course, an ancient device and is not something which has arisen while the present government has been in power. You know, Mr. Speaker, I always like to go back into history whenever I am faced with a particular problem. If I have the time I like to read the history of the past in order to appreciate what has happened in the past. I think this is of great assistance in giving consideration to the matters of the moment.
I find, Mr. Speaker, that the first record of a combine is in the Bible. When Esau returned famished from the hunt and went to Jacob to get some food, Jacob had a complete monopoly on the food supply and in order to get a decent meal Esau had to sell his birthright. In reading history I find that people in all nations have been selling their birthright ever since to monopolies and combines in order to get a chance to live.
A second illustration is that of Joseph getting a monopoly of the grain industry in Egypt. The people were starving, and he set the price so high that they spent all their cash buying grain in the first year, and in the second year the poor people of Egypt had to sell all their flocks, cattle and asses in order to live. The same thing has gone on all through history.
I also find that for over 1,000 years the merchants of Tyre and Sidon had a complete monopoly of trade, prices and distribution in the Mediterranean area. If you go into the matter carefully you will find that most of the wars of that time were fought as a result of the greed of these monopolists in

the early days of marketing and merchandising. When we come to the middle ages we find that combines arose then to control the marketing of goods and to control prices and, just after the plague in Great Britain, to control wages. A few people got together in their own interests, which is very natural. When we are dealing with this question we should always say to ourselves, "Let him that is without sin cast the first stone".
I mention these things to indicate what an ancient device this has been, and that it has continued throughout history. People have combined together for their own advantage. Then we come to the situation in the United States in more recent times. We know the history of the early development of industry in the United States involving transportation and the development of natural resources. The whole history is sordid and soiled with illustrations of a few persons getting together, combining and creating a monopoly for their own advantage to the disadvantage of the great majority of the people of the country.
That was what caused a former president of the United States, Teddy Roosevelt, to start his "trust-busting" mission, because they became so vicious in the early part of this century. The legislation that resulted from his efforts had some effect in preventing the further development of the grosser aspects of trusts, combines and monopolies at that time. It was not finally effective because they always find new ways of dealing with the problem of control, as they have done in Canada all through history.
All one needs to do is look at the combines and monopolies formed by the armament manufacturers. A former leader of the Progressive Conservative party, Mr. Drew, in a series of articles in Maclean's magazine prior to the second world war termed them "salesmen of death". Just read the history of the armament manufacturers in Europe and in other countries of the world, and you will see how these people got together, combined to get top prices and find markets, and even promoted wars. In the context of that development you have the Krupp armament industry in Germany, which we were told at the end of the war would be taken away from them and given to the German people. But the same people are still in possession, and if the same trend continues that continued prior to the first world war, the same monopoly of these instruments of war, it will result in war again.
What about combines in our country? As the minister mentioned, the first legislative approach to this question was in 1899, I believe.

Combines Investigation Act there were combines in the glassware industry, the packing industry, the milling industry, the flour industry, the rubber industry and so on, and in the food industry generally. But regardless of their good work throughout the years their efforts have been largely ineffective. They have not produced results because, regardless of all this work, within the framework of the combines investigation legislation monopoly control of markets, patents and prices is growing stronger and stronger every year.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that my attention was first focused on the monopoly situation as a result of practices in the fruit industry. I was a director of a co-operative society in the fruit industry shortly after the first world war and on into the 1930's. We discovered that something was wrong-we were nearly all starving-that we were being fleeced right and left by the managers of United States controlled companies that were distributing fruit on the prairies.
I will give you a couple of illustrations in order to show what happens when these people have control over fruit products. This is a typical illustration. I had a neighbour by the name of Sam Hall, a hard-working old gentleman who, before we formed the co-operative and before we had this investigation, started off for Calgary with a carload of McIntosh apples. He arrived in Calgary intending to sell his apples to the jobbers there. One jobber offered him a certain price; I think he offered him $1 a box or $1.25 a box in Calgary. The car was on the siding. He said, "Oh, no, I am not going to sell for that price". He then went to another jobber. He spent two days in going around to six jobbers. The first jobber telephoned to his friends and said, "This man Sam Hall called on me. If we all stick tight together we will get his apples for 70 cents a box and we will split the profit". That is just what happened. Sam Hall was paying demurrage. He was a man who could not afford to stay at an hotel for long, and at the end of the second day he sold his carload of apples for 70 cents and those distributors of fruit shared the profits.
Another friend of mine was determined that he would sell direct to the prairie farmers. He took a carload of apples into Moose Jaw, or out on a spur at some little town close to Moose Jaw. He arrived there on a Friday afternoon and advertised apples for sale directly from the car at a dollar a box. At that price he would have done fairly well. He had 800 boxes in the car. At least he would have obtained enough or the price would have been sufficient so that when he sold his crop he would have had something

on which to live. But what happened? The fruit wholesalers in Moose Jaw had him pinched that Friday night for selling fruit without a licence. They had him arrested and brought before the justice of the peace. Then he was told that his case could not be heard until Tuesday morning. In the meantime one big wholesale house in Moose Jaw had a carload of apples shipped to the siding where his car was located, and they offered the apples to the farmers at 75 cents a box off the car. When my friend was tried on Tuesday morning, of course, he was released because he had the right to sell apples. He was the grower of the product he was selling, and under the provincial law at that time he had a perfect right to sell the apples. But in the meantime his market was taken away from him by the sale of these other apples at 75 cents a box. He was therefore obliged to practically give his apples away and return home.
It was as a result of that kind of practice or monopoly that the growers insisted on an investigation into alleged combines in the distribution of fruit and vegetables in 1924. An investigation was held under the Combines Investigation Act. A report was made on February 18, 1925 by the commissioner Mr. Lewis Duncan, who was a prominent lawyer in Toronto at that time. I remember him quite well in this field because I did all I could to help provide evidence from the growers' point of view.
I use these illustrations in order to show what monopolies and combines will do without any consideration for the persons whose livelihood depends upon food production, and without any consideration for the consumer.
I will just read some extracts from a brief letter in this report, because it shows the vileness of these people; and these things are easily forgotten. This letter was written by Mr. G. H. Snow, manager of the Mutual Fruit Company of Vancouver. His name might be Snow but he was far from being white, Mr. Speaker. I just want to read this to bring to the attention of some of the prairie members who are particularly interested in the problems of grain growers the fact that the fruit growers also have their problems, and they are at times very difficult ones indeed. He says:
We have four men at work in the Hatzic district, including two directors, and we are sure that each one of the four has no idea that the others are wearing our brand. We think it will be quite in order to commit any crime, murder excepted, to land this Hatzic bunch as a unit, on the same basis as Gilland and Tanner. We are proceeding to do this, irrespective of how much it will cost, because once we get them they are ours for keeps. No matter what happens we must use the greatest of

care, in case our plans fall down and the Central operates again in 1924, to see that we still appear to have clean hands when we ask for the deal.
Then later the same gentleman goes on in another letter to say:
As far as we are concerned things are brightening daily on the berry deal. There is a possibility that we will get our views into Farm and Home-
That was the farmers' magazine in British Columbia.
-through an advertisement of Gilland's. We will not stand for the ad's going in edited by Farm and Home and it will have to go in as we have written it, as we are paying for it. Gilland wants to reach a section of the growers that are strong for co-operation, no matter what the cost.
We believe that we will have the handling of the rhubarb of the Dewdney association this year. This is the crowd that the growers sales had last year. It will amount to from 17 to 20 cars.
The whole of the evidence contained in this book shows the skulduggery of these people who had no regard for the producers and no regard for the consumers. It was as a result of this report that Tree Fruits Limited was formed in British Columbia and the growers' association received a measure of protection under the British Columbia tree fruits marketing act.
Even to this day the great tree fruits organizations or the co-operatives cannot sell to any other co-operative in Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba. And do you know why, Mr. Speaker? It is because the growers have their own brokers but not their own wholesalers, and that is a very expensive business on account of the cold storage costs involved. If a British Columbia grower goes to a co-operative or retailer in Alberta or Saskatchewan, for example, and says, "We would like you to buy from us direct", the possible purchaser will say, "I am sorry, I cannot; because if I buy my apples from you the wholesalers will not supply us with citrus fruits, nuts and oranges, and other things from across the line".
Mr. Speaker, I just mention this to show how the tendency to combine has found expression in our country throughout the years. All through the ages efforts have been made to curb monopolies. As I said before I give the minister and all those who have made efforts in this direction through the Combines Investigation Act and so on full credit, but to date these efforts have on the whole been completely ineffective and unsuccessful.
The practice of monopoly control is an ancient vice with which every civilization to date has had to contend. Because I am dealing with the principle of the problem rather than the details of the bill, with which my colleagues have dealt very fully indeed, I would like to quote from an edict issued by
Combines Investigation Act the Emperor Zeno to the praetorian prefect of Constantinople, A.D. 483, to show how the problem was then:
We command that no one may presume to exercise a monopoly of any kind of clothing or of fish or of any other thing serving for food, or for any other use ... nor may any persons combine or agree in unlawful meetings, that different kinds of merchandise may not be sold at a less price than they have agreed upon among themselves. Workmen and contractors for building, and all who practice other professions, and contractors for baths, are entirely prohibited from agreeing together ... and if any one shall presume to practice a monopoly, let his property be forfeited and himself condemned to perpetual exile.
I wish the minister would include that penalty in the Combines Investigation Act; then we would get somewhere. Even the Christian church in the early days spoke out very strongly against usury, that is, monopoly of credit and high interest rates, and the monopoly of the distribution of goods, and it supported price control and regulation. All through the middle ages numerous laws were passed to overcome the effects of combines and monopolies. As I said before, in the United States we had the "trust-busting" campaign of the late president, Theodore Roosevelt, and then in Canada we had the Combines Investigation Act of 1910. While it was effective in a limited way, the record proves that to date under the free enterprise or private ownership system, methods to control the practices of monopolies and combines have been ineffective.
Before proceeding further, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I have read with interest the minister's speech, and I am sure he spent a considerable time on it. I noticed the very careful wording on page 4344 of Hansard in which he preaches the new conservatism which, on reading it over carefully, sounds like the liberalism of 1910 in Great Britain. The minister said, as reported on page 4344 of Hansard:
The basic principle is that a free enterprise system is the system which will yield the highest material standard of living in conjunction with the greatest possible degree of political, economic and social freedom for the individual and that this system of free enterprise will be best maintained through the operation and preservation of active competition between the various sectors of the economy.
I am sure that when the minister says that he believes it, but the trouble is that while he is saying that, and has been preaching free enterprise and the control of monopolies for years, the fact is that every day they have been strengthening their ownership of natural resources and of manufacturing capacity in Canada. These rights are passing into fewer and fewer hands; there is no question about that.
I was also interested in the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, and in fact I was

Combines Investigation Act a bit startled. As reported on page 4353 of Hansard he had this to say:
We on this side believe that in the circumstances Canada faces today and has faced now for a good many years, a mixed economic system is the most appropriate form of economic organization for the development of our country; a mixed economic system composed of a public sector, a co-operative sector and a private enterprise sector.
By George, I am sure he must have pinched that out of one of our speeches of some time ago. He continued:
We also believe that the private enterprise sector should be as large but only as large as compatible with the public interest-
That is a typical qualification. You leave yourself in a perfect position to manoeuvre under varying circumstances.
-and that it should be governed by the competitive rule applied in free markets, having regard, however, as the minister mentioned during his speech, to the changing nature of economic circumstances and the changing nature of economic development.
I want to congratulate, in the first instance, the Leader of the Official Opposition for taking a plank from the C.C.F. platform. If he continues in that direction the only thing he can possibly do is join the C.C.F. party, because we are the only party in this house that has preached the doctrine of the mixed or dual economy. Since I have been in the house this has never been mentioned by a Liberal speaker and used as a plank in the Liberal platform.

Let me say this, however. Regardless of the statements of these people, under the Liberal and Conservative governments, that is under capitalism-and I am not blaming individuals-monopolists have continued to thrive and expand. Not only that, but they have become more powerful every day. Control of Canadian resources, Canadian banking institutions and Canadian manufacturing has fallen increasingly into fewer and fewer hands.

That is the situation today. In this connection I want to quote from a book by Mr. H. Percy Scott which was published in 1915. The book is entitled "The New Slavery" and its author was dealing with this very question of monopolies, which was at that time of serious concern to governments and to the people. This is what Mr. Scott wrote in 1915:
There can be no reasonable doubt that the production of food in Canada and the United States is ample to provide all of the inhabitants with plenty at the lowest prices.
The causes commonly alleged for the prevailing high prices will not bear the slightest scrutiny.
The experience of England and France proves that prices can be kept fairly stable where laws against extortion through combines and monopolies prevail.
In Canada, the United States and Germany, where such laws are not enforced, great distress results therefrom.
This is the greatest question of the day and the one most vitally affecting the great body of people that has come up since confederation. As we have seen, there have been many theories regarding it propounded, and views of it have been made from almost every conceivable point of view. These pages will have been written not in vain if they have demonstrated in any measure the folly of neglecting or allowing to fall into abeyance laws affecting the people's rights which have stood the test of centuries.
That was in 1915. Regardless of the good intentions of governments since that day we are still faced with the problem, as is clear from the introduction of amendments by the minister to the Combines Investigation Act. I would say that the proof of the pudding is in the eating, and it is obvious that to date we have had no effective control. Monopoly of political power has been- broken by centuries of struggle in the western nations, the result of which has been the development of democracy and parliamentary institutions. However, in the opinion of this group these institutions can become a facade and a sham if economic power becomes the prerogative of only the few. Fascism was the direct result of economic royalists' fear of the people and their wish to perpetuate and extend monopoly control.
As I see it, the world moves in advancing cycles; and I should like the minister to listen to my argument from now on, because I think he may well be in agreement with at least the principles I expound. First we have the political and economic monopolies of the ancient world up to the middle ages. Then we have the competitive spirit of the industrial revolution which soon develop into monopoly control and, to some extent, the restriction of competition. In the middle ages we find public control and the regulation of prices, wages and markets. The doctrine of a fair price and a fair day's wage for a fair day's work was supported by the ancient church according to the principles of the

gospel as they were understood at that time. These principles became part of the canon law of the ancient church and the church in the middle ages, particularly toward the end of the fifteenth century.
Modern industrial nations have passed through a period of industrial expansion with almost complete freedom for monopolists with regard to the ownership of natural resources, the control of patents, prices, markets and so on. No legislation adopted to date, however well intentioned, has provided effective control of monopolies and combines. The disease is still with us, as it was with the ancient Greeks. I suggest that in Canada we are now entering upon a cycle in history that demands legislation which will provide effective control of our economic development by the representatives of the people for the people. I also suggest that the economic doctrine of the canonists of the middle ages- I said "economic doctrine"-finds its modem expression in the policies and programs of the C.C.F., the socialists. That means the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation in Canada.

The field in which the emotion giving rise to the attacks on the bill has been most apparent is that part of the bill which seeks to give a measure of protection to small business against the damaging and unfair competitive practices which are sometimes engaged in by their big competitors. It is for this reason that I said just before one o'clock, and I repeat now, that it appears that the division which, if we are to take at their face value the things which have been said by the opposition we can safely assume will be coming, will show us on which side stand those who are prepared to do something to protect small business and on which side stand those who are prepared to talk about it but when the issue comes up and the opportunity is presented to do something about it, align themselves against small business and in favour of leaving them at the mercy of their large competitors.
Those, of course, are not the only issues in this legislation, but those are the issues in the main upon which the opposition has chosen to take its stand in its criticisms of the legislation. It is a fact that for years the Liberal party when it was in power, and now again in this debate, has shown itself ready to talk about the interests of small

Combines Investigation Act business and in sympathy with their position; but, Mr. Speaker, there is only one way you can protect small business and that is by doing something about it. We have brought in legislation designed to do something about it, and now we find that when the opportunity is presented to decide for or against doing something about small business it is clear that the Conservative party and the Conservative government is prepared to do something while those in opposition are prepared only to talk.
