I am always humble, Mr. Speaker. We on this side still remember that we are not a government of supermen as our predecessors believed they were. It was obvious that the Leader of the Opposition was irritated by that attempt of mine to put the historical record before the house in its proper perspective. The hon. gentleman therefore undertook to read me a small lecture in history and of course, bearing in mind that my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition was an eminent historian before he became a politician, I think in this context I can only say it is obvious that the hon. member is now a better politician than he is a historian, because he repeated the mythological error of the Liberal party that the Conservatives' efforts over the years have been directed to weakening the combines legislation. I therefore feel it is desirable again to give the house a brief review of what are the historical facts in this regard.
I point out again that it was a Conservative government that first introduced anticombines legislation in Canada and placed the first bill on the statute books in 1889. In 1892 that law was redefined, and it is that law which virtually without change stands today as the central working definition of a combine. It is that definition now found in section 409 and 411 of the Criminal Code under which the great majority of combines prosecutions and convictions have been secured.
It is true that in the legislation enacted in 1892 there was no special machinery provided for investigation or administration, which were left to the ordinary processes of the criminal law.
It is also true that in 1910 the Liberal government introduced a Combines Investigation Act. This bill supplied a special machinery for investigation to supplement the ordinary machinery of criminal investigation, but this act had two important weaknesses especially when you assess it in the light of the present combines legislation. First, it imposed on private citizens the considerable responsibility and expense of initiating investigation; second, it provided no continuity in the administration of the legislation.

It was left to a Conservative government again to remedy those important defects.
In 1919 the Conservative government set up a special committee of the House of Commons, which in turn recommended the improvement of the legislation by the establishment of a permanent board to administer the laws relating to trade combinations and monopolies, and further legislation relating to profiteering and hoarding. As a result, the government of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen introduced legislation known as the board of commerce act and the combines and fair prices act, implementing the recommendations of the committee of the House of Commons. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the privy council declared some parts of that legislation ultra vires. That declaration related particularly to those parts of the legislation which gave the government power to take direct action by way of controlling the abuses of profiteering and hoarding.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker-again it is necessary to consider the legislation in the light of the economic conditions of the time after world war I, when this legislation was enacted-that profiteering and hoarding were real problems. The Conservative government did not hesitate to deal with them, and the only weakness of the legislation was that it went too far by way of giving direct power to the government to take steps in those fields. It was for those reasons that the legislation was declared ultra vires.
Lest there be any doubt as to whether the Conservative government was prepared to take effective action in this field, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer the house to the findings in the MacQuarrie committee report. I do this because the Leader of the Opposition sought to belittle this legislation of 1919, and to use it as an example to prove his myth that Conservative governments have traditionally been opposed to anti-combines legislation. I should like to refer my hon. friend to the findings of the MacQuarrie committee, a committee set up by the government of which he was a member. Those findings with regard to the 1919 legislation, as reported on pages 11 and 12 of the MacQuarrie committee report, read:
The act in its second part prohibited hoarding and profiteering.
This seems to me a strange thing to find in an act which is represented by my hon. friends as something designed to take the teeth out of combines legislation. I continue:
The board was empowered and directed to inquire into and to restrain and prohibit any breach or non-observance of the act. the making of unfair profits, and all such practices with respect to the holding or disposition of the necessaries of life, as, in the opinion of the board, were calculated to enhance their cost or price.
Combines Investigation Act
As I say, Mr. Speaker, that is a queer sort of thing to find in legislation which my hon. friends opposite characterized as a typical attempt of a Conservative government to take the teeth out of combines legislation. The only fault with that legislation was that it went too far in respect of the powers it sought to give to the government to deal with this problem. But here is the other interesting finding of the MacQuarrie committee as contained on page 12 of their report:
It is to be observed that the legislation overcame two of the principal defects of the act of 1910-
The act of 1910, I may remind the house, was an act of the Liberal government. I continue:
-namely the absence of a continuing enforcement authority and the initiation of investigations only on the application of interested private individuals.
Therefore you will see, Mr. Speaker, that a reading of history, supplemented in this case by a reading of the report of an impartial committee set up by a Liberal government confirms that the attempts of the Conservative government have been to strengthen and make realistic the anti-combines legislation of Canada. If this is not to be accepted by my hon. friends opposite let me remind them that when in 1923 the Liberal government re-enacted the combines legislation they took almost in their entirety the provisions which had been contained in the act of 1919, to which I have been referring and which were not declared ultra vires, and those additional provisions relating to administration and enforcement of the legislation remain still the basis of that part of the present anti-combines legislation.
My hon. friends, in their distortion of history, attempted to suggest that the legislation of the Bennett government in 1935 was a further attempt to take the teeth out of the combines law. Now, Mr. Speaker, a reading of history and the facts of history establishes that far from that being the case, the legislation introduced in 1935 was an honest and far-reaching attempt to deal with the economic situation of that day; was indeed based upon the report of a parliamentary committee which became a royal commission of that day, a royal commission of which my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition was secretary, as he himself reminded us. In this connection I could perhaps remind the house briefly of what I said in my opening remarks on Monday of last week as to the effects of the bill. It seeks to do three things. First, it seeks to clarify and consolidate the legislation. Second, it seeks to

bring a measure of protection to the legitimate interests of small business. Third, it seeks to make the legislation more flexible in the light of the mid-twentieth century economy, both with respect to what it accomplishes by way of clarification and with respect to the new procedures for enforcement which are provided. Having ignored these objectives of the bill, it is quite understandable that the criticisms made by the opposition would be, as they are in my submission, unfounded and misdirected.
The Leader of the Opposition suggested that all that should be done or that all that requires to be done lies within the scope of administrative changes, and he listed three things. First, he said the government should take care to make sure that the director does not abuse his powers. Second, he said that reports of the commission should contain recommendations for alternative remedies, that is to say remedies alternative to prosecution. Third, he said there should be emphasis upon research in this field in addition to enforcement.
It is interesting to note that two of these three recommendations were contained in the MacQuarrie committee report. That report was brought down some five years before the government of which my hon. friend was a member was dismissed from office. It is therefore interesting to find that, even in spite of that fact, my hon. friend still is suggesting that these are the changes that should be made, and the only changes that should be made. It does not speak very highly of his opinion of what his government was doing during that last five years of office. He accused us of introducing three new principles which he described as damaging to the content of the legislation. It does this because we believe that in the mid-twentieth century, and in the type of competitive economy in which we exist, it is essential to encourage business to do those things which it can do without damage to the economy and which, if done, will produce positive benefits to the economy and to the consumers of Canada domestically, and will enable business to compete more effectively in international markets. He said: Mr. Speaker, when the resolution preceding this present bill was before the committee I gave a detailed statement of the background of the problem and of the reasons which prompted the government to recommend to the house these present amendments. I also gave an outline of the nature of these amendments and of the effects which they would have in permitting all pensioners who leave Canada to continue to receive their pension for a minimum period of six months, as well as making it possible for the vast majority of pensioners who leave Canada to continue to receive their pensions for an indefinite period of time.
I do not propose to repeat all that I said in the course of my statement on the resolution, but I might perhaps repeat the four main effects of the present legislation:
1.	By repealing section 5 (1) of the present Old Age Security Act these new amendments will do away with the requirement that an old age security pension must be suspended when a pensioner absents himself from Canada for a period in excess of one month. Henceforth, no recipient of old age security will have his pension suspended when he leaves Canada.
2.	The new section 5(1), contained in clause 1 of the amending bill, will substitute for the present provision-requiring immediate suspension of pension-a new procedure which will in effect permit pension payments to be continued in all cases of departure from Canada for a minimum period of six full months of absence in addition to the month in which the pensioner leaves Canada. This new provision will apply to all pensioners who leave Canada regardless of the length of their previous residence in the country.
3.	The new section 5(1) will also provide that in the case of pensioners who have resided in Canada 25 years or more after their 21st birthday there will be no limit whatever on the length of the period during which they may continue to receive their pensions outside of Canada.
4.	Only in the case of pensioners who have less than 25 years' residence in Canada following their 21st birthday will the six-month limit to which I have already referred have any effect. Such persons, instead of having their pensions suspended as soon as they leave Canada-which is the requirement under the present law-will receive their pension cheques in the normal way for the month of their departure and will continue to have their pension cheques mailed to them wherever they may be outside of Canada for a further period of absence up to a maximum of six consecutive months in addition to the actual month of their departure. If, in the

seventh month following the month of their departure, they return to Canada their pension payment will be paid as usual and will be continued thereafter without any interruption whatever. In the event, however, that they do not return to Canada before the end of the seventh month following the month of their departure pension payments will be suspended and will be resumed only with effect from the month in which they actually return.
I have already explained in my statement on the resolution why it is that the government considers that a distinction should be made between the periods of absence permitted in the case of those individuals with long periods of residence in Canada and the somewhat shorter period of absence permitted in the case of those who have relatively short periods of residence in the country. Both groups of pensioners-those with shorter periods of residence, as well as those with longer periods-will receive substantially more generous treatment than is possible under the present legislation, but no limits of any kind will be placed on the periods of absence permitted to those pensioners who have resided in Canada for at least 25 years after attaining their 21st birthday.
I feel confident that the principles which the government has recommended for inclusion in the legislation will commend themselves generally to the members of the house.
Some question may be raised as to the reason why the period of 25 years has been stipulated, and I think I can explain this by pointing out that this period represents approximately one half of what might normally be regarded as an individual's active working life between the time when he attains his majority and the time when he reaches the age of 70 years which the Old Age Security Act assumes to be the point of full retirement.
I might also say a word about the purpose of the supplementary provisions contained in clauses 2 and 3 of the amending legislation. In clause 2 we are concerned with the position of pensioners who may be absent from Canada on the day when the amending legislation comes into effect and who if they return to Canada within the time limits specified by section 5(1) of the present legislation would be entitled to pick up certain retroactive payments for the months during which they had been absent.
If clause 2 of the amending bill were not included there might be some doubt as to the position of these returning pensioners with respect to the retroactive payments to which they are entitled under the present

Old Age Security Act
legislation. We wish to make it absolutely clear through clause 2 of the amending bill that returning pensioners will be fully protected with respect to any retroactive payments that they might have been entitled to pick up, covering the months of their absence, under the existing legislation.
Clause 3 of the amending bill is also transitional in character and is designed to cover the position of a pensioner who is out of Canada at the time when the new legislation becomes effective, and who continues to remain outside of Canada for a further period following the passage of the new legislation. Any such individuals who have the required 25 years' residence in Canada following their 21st birthday may, without returning to Canada, make application to have their pension payments resumed, and if found to be eligible for such resumption of payments they will be reinstated with effect from the first day of the month when the amending legislation comes into force.
No time limit is set in the making of such application. It does not matter whether such a pensioner files his application in the month following the passage of the legislation or six months later or a year later. In all cases, the applicant, if found to be eligible for reinstatement, will be reinstated with effect from the month in which the new legislation comes into force.
I might mention in this connection that there is no provision in the amending bill specifying the date upon which the new legislation becomes effective, or providing that the legislation shall become effective only upon proclamation. In consequence it will be clear that the amending legislation will come into force on the day when it receives royal assent.
It will be noted that the provision contained in clause 3 of the amending bill applies only to those pensioners who are outside of Canada on the day when the act comes into effect and who can establish that at the time they left Canada they had resided in Canada at least 25 years after reaching the age of 21.
Of course, it may well be asked, what happens in the case of a pensioner with fewer than 25 years of residence in Canada after his 21st birthday who happens to be absent from Canada on the day when this new act comes into force? Such a pensioner will not, of course, be entitled to apply for reinstatement of his pension in absentia but when he returns to Canada clause 2 of the amending legislation will apply and he will receive any pension payments in respect of the period of his absence which he would have been entitled to receive under the provisions of the existing legislation.

I think I should perhaps leave to the committee stage of the bill any further explanations which might be required with respect to the more detailed provisions of the various clauses, as well as any explanations which might be desired with respect to the more detailed procedures we propose to put into effect in the actual administration of the new provisions.
It will be appreciated that the old age security administration will now for the first time be faced with the requirement of sending old age security payments outside of Canada to persons who may move to any other country in the world. This will present a number of new problems to the administration, but fortunately we will be able to call upon the experience of other branches of the government service which have already had to deal with this problem. I might mention in this connection the annuities branch of the Department of Labour, the Canadian pension commission, the superannuation branch of the Department of Finance, all of which have had a considerable experience in issuing payments of one kind or another to beneficiaries in other countries.
It is not expected that the problems to be faced by the old age security administration will be in any important respects different from those which have already been successfully handled by the agencies to which I have referred. It is, of course, true that the volume of payments to old age security pensioners outside of Canada is likely to be substantially greater than in the other programs which I have mentioned.
While it is difficult to estimate for the years ahead the extent to which this amendment will result in increased expenditures, on the basis of experience to date it would appear that the cost in the initial years may be of the order of $2 million or $3 million annually.
In the discussion of the resolution the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) raised the question of proof of age. His complimentary comments concerning the sympathetic understanding with which this matter has been dealt is appreciated and I can assure him that this practice will continue. He also mentioned the question of proof of residence in determining the 25 years of residence and asked whether 25 years would have to be a continuous period. As he will note, now that he has the proposed amendment before him, it only requires that a pensioner has resided in Canada for 25 years after attaining the age of 21 years. In other words, it is not necessary for the 25 years to be a continuous period of time.
If this amendment receives approval it will, of course, be necessary to amend the regulations under the Old Age Security Act to take

into account this change. While consideration of the regulations must await the passage of this amendment, it would be my hope and expectation that the approach to be followed would be consistent with the existing regulations relating to residence provisions for the purpose of qualifying for pension. For example, present regulations provide for continuation of residence in special cases such as for members of the armed forces when they have to spend part of their service outside of Canada; also, there is provision for periods of temporary absence prior to application which are deemed not to interrupt residence. Considerations such as these would have to be taken into account when the regulations are being amended with respect to the 25-year residence requirement after age 21.

I have some figures as to the number of pensioners who may be affected. We have in excess of 850,000 old age security recipients on our pension rolls at the present time. Actually for the month of March the number of pensioners totalled 876,410. It should be kept in mind in this connection that the vast majority of these pensioners qualified for old age security benefit at a time prior to 1957 when the requirement was not less than 20 years' residence in Canada. Even in the case of those pensioners who have come on the rolls since the residence requirement was reduced in 1957 from 20 to 10 years, the vast majority

Old Age Security Act
of them have well in excess of 20 years' residence in this country. From this it will be seen that the great majority of pensioners presently on the rolls, or likely to come on the rolls in the future, would have no difficulty in establishing that they have resided in Canada 25 years or more following their attainment of the age of 21.
It may interest the house to know that we have made an analysis of some 2,696 pensioners who in February of this year were known to be permanently absent from Canada. A review of the individual files revealed that in 77.7 per cent of all cases, or 2,095, the pensioners possessed the required number of years residence after the age of 21 to qualify them for a lifetime pension. Only 3.7 per cent, or 100 pensioners, on the basis of the residence history already on file had less than 25 years' residence in Canada after the age of 21. The remaining 18.7 per cent, or 501 cases, were cases in which a precise determination of the residence status could not be made from the evidence on file, since these cases had been transferred from provincial old age assistance rolls and detailed status so far as residence was concerned could only be determined by reference to the original residence history contained in the provincial records.
It would seem, on the basis of these figures, however, safe to assume that well over 80 per cent of all pensioners will have no difficulty in establishing that they have 25 years or more of residence in Canada following their 21st birthday, and it may well be that experience will show that this percentage will be closer to 90 per cent than to 80 per cent of all cases.
Fortunately, of course, for the administration, not all of these old age pensioners will leave Canada either for temporary or for permanent periods of absence, and thus the number of cases in which pension payments will henceforth have to be made outside of Canada will be very much smaller than the 876,410 cases which I have mentioned.
In actual fact, we have made an analysis covering a 21-month period from January 1, 1958 to September 30, 1959 which shows that slightly more than 24,000 pensioners left Canada during this period to spend from one to six months outside of Canada, but returned in time to avoid any loss of pension under the law as it existed at that time. All of those 24,000 cases experienced, of course, under the existing law a suspension of pension during the period of their absence and picked up their pension payments for the months of their absence when they returned. The figure of 24,000 to which I have referred

works out to an average of approximately 1,160 departures each month.
I would point out that in all of these cases where the pensioner left Canada and returned within a six-month period the new amendments will provide uninterrupted payments of pension during the period of temporary absence.
I can also report that in the same 21-month period-January 1, 1958 to September 30, 1959-some 441 pensioners overstayed their leave and forfeited one or more months of pension in respect of the period of their absence under the law at it then existed. This works out to an average of 22 cases a month of persons who returned to Canada after extended periods of absence lasting more than six months and who, under the existing law, would forfeit at least a portion of their pension. I hope that answers the hon. member's question.

speechtext: Is it not apparent from those figures that it would be a relatively insignificant figure?

speechtext: It might be an insignificant figure. I would not say it was insignificant. The vast majority of people would be able to qualify if it were reduced to 10 years. There would not be, possibly, more than 10 to 20 per cent, which would be some 80,000 or 160,000, who might be able to qualify under those terms. I still feel, however, that the citizens of Canada would not like it, at this stage at least, if a resident who retired from some other country came to Canada, for argument's sake, at 60 years of age, lived here for 10 years and took a fully qualified pension back to some other country.

It is not a question of whether one agrees or not. The fact is that that was the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were on this side of the house and now, as in so many other instances, they do not observe their own recommendations.

It is pleasant to be able to carry on a discussion of these points in almost an informal way. I still think it would be just and fair to all concerned, since the act at the moment says that after a period of 10 years a person has sufficient equity either by monetary contribution or physical contribution or in some other way to draw a pension-if we are going to adopt the principle of this proposed bill in the clause we are adopting now, that a person is eligible to receive a pension within certain limits outside Canada-that we should certainly act accordingly. After 10 years we say, a person is eligible for a pension at the age of 70. Surely, it naturally follows that if we are going to say to some percentage of those who are liable for that pension that they can receive it and live outside Canada, we should say that to the rest of them and make it uniformly applicable. That is the suggestion
1	make. It is in that sense.
This would prevent the establishment of two types of old age pensioners with different standards of qualification referred to by the minister. Perhaps the minister says, "At one stage we reduced the qualifying period from 20 to 10 years and at another increased the income tax contribution from
2	to 3 per cent and this division into two groups of people, or possibly three, justifies the present division." If that is the reason for the establishment of two pension groups that is a different thing again. Perhaps the minister would tell us what bearing this had on the selection of the 25-year period.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I think we should go back to the time when old age security was 79951-0-288
Old Age Security Act
established in 1951 at $40 a month. At that time there was put on a 2-2-2 formula, 2 per cent of sales tax, 2 per cent of income tax and 2 per cent of corporation tax. There was no equity at all at that time. In other words, the people who were qualified were paid the amount of money monthly as a pension. I do not think anybody at that time argued that from then on it was completely contributory.
In 1957 some adjustments were made to the act. The 20-year qualifying period was reduced to 10 and the period of permissible absence was increased from 3 to 6 months. The pension was raised to $55 with no change in the 2-2-2 formula. As of a year ago the Minister of Finance announced an increase in the formula from 2-2-2 to 3-3-3 which provided more money to the pension fund. I believe the hon. gentleman mentioned in his last budget address that there would probably be a surplus in the fund this year.
In my opening remarks at the resolution stage I said that as time progressed people felt they had developed some equity in the fund. Everyone is subject to the pension whether or not they contribute to it and indeed they contribute automatically by way of sales tax, of course. Regardless of whether they pay personal income tax they still receive the benefit of the pension. It has been felt that if over the years they have contributed in one way or another to the welfare and development of Canada-if they contributed for 25 years of their so-called working life, if you want to put it that way, the half-way period between ages 21 and 70- they should be entitled to take the pension with them out of the country. I do not think I could go any further.
I still feel that a person who may retire at age 60, let us say for argument's sake, in some other country and who comes to Canada at age 60 and lives here and who may or may not contribute anything-he may not be in a taxable bracket and not contribute anything-
He would contribute by way of the sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, everybody does that but I was referring to his not contributing by way of personal income tax. He may do so, and I am not saying he does not. I still do not feel it would be proper for him to come and live here for 10 years, let us say, and then take the pension back to his native country.

As a result of a letter I received last Saturday from a constituent who left for the United Kingdom a few months ago to visit his son I am curious about the effect of clause 1 on the circumstances

Old Age Security Act
he relates. He had heard of the intention to pass legislation along these lines. Through a letter written on his behalf he states that it was his intention to come back to Canada but while in the United Kingdom he suffered a stroke. He doubts that his physical condition will permit him to return to Canada. I read the explanatory notes to the bill and am wondering if he will be entitled to his pension if he does not return to this country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What is his category so far as-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Has he lived here 25
years since age 21?

speechtext: Then he will get his pension.

1. (a) that any pensioner who leaves Canada following the passage of the amendment-
And then if you look at subparagraph (b) of the explanatory notes it opens with the words:
1. (b) that any such pensioner-
I take it that "any such pensioner" is a pensioner who leaves Canada following the passage of the amendment. It would seem to me very unjust-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Clause 3, I think, covers that. He will receive the full effect of the present legislation as well.
I am glad to hear it. It may be that the man's health will not permit him to return to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He will not have to return in order to receive the pension.

Mr. Chairman, we want to ascertain from the minister why the period of 25 years has been selected. I suggest that a person who was here 20 years after attaining his 21st birthday would in principle certainly be as justified in receiving the benefit of this amendment as one who had been here 25 years. How did we arrive at the figure 25? Why did we leave out those who have been here for 15 or 20 years? What are the numbers of people it is estimated will be covered in those categories? If it is justifiable, as I believe it is, to do this for those who have been here 25

years after attaining their 21st birthday I believe in principle it will be difficult to justify not extending it to others.
It is true that the present Old Age Security Act is not fully contributory. As the minister said, it is partially contributory based on contributions through the sales tax, the income tax and the corporation tax and individuals who are here for any period before attaining the right to benefit do make contributions in all of these three forms or in one of them. Everyone regardless of the length of time spent in the country does make a contribution toward the sales tax which is by no means an inconsequential source of revenue.
If this particular proposal is justified in principle, as I believe it is now, I should like a more precise explanation from the minister as to why the principle is not extended to categories other than those who have spent 25 years after their 21st birthday in Canada. Certainly the person who has spent 20 years in Canada does not come within the mischief of the criticism made by the minister about those who had spent 10 years, who had come here at the age of 60. I think the same would apply to those who had been here 15 years. As a matter of fact, I find it very difficult to accept the view that if it is right in principle it should not extend to those who are as a matter of right now in receipt of a pension.
I know it is not easy to arrive at those solutions but, having accepted the principle, as the minister has done, that there is a right of a retired person to carry his old age security benefit with him wherever he goes; having established that as a principle of acceptance-and this is what the minister did when he presented the legislation-it seems to me he has not made out a satisfactory case for refusing to extend it to all who have won the right in law to receive the old age security pension.
For the same reason that you made it 20 years and not 19 or 18.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the government feels that this legislation is very fair. As the hon. member for Essex East has pointed out, this has not been completely contributory. It has been on a contributory basis of any nature only since 1952. It is felt that a person who has contributed one half of his presumable working life, up until what might be called the compulsory retiring age of 70, to the development of Canada by way of taxes and otherwise over the period prior to the contributory feature entering into the picture is entitled to this extra concern. A person who has given all those years of service to Canada in one way or another and

has contributed to the development of Canada in one way or another and by taxes is entitled to this extra consideration. I think that answers the question, Mr. Chairman.

May I pose a question to the minister? May I set up a sort of hypothetical circumstance and see whether this is what would apply? As I read this it seems to me that one would be able to come to one or two conclusions. Under the proposed legislation could a pensioner absent himself for six continuous months and continue to receive the pension? I refer to one that does not fall within paragraph (b), the 25-year qualification. I refer to someone who has not resided here for 25 years but returns to Canada upon the conclusion of the six months and lives here for another one or two months and then absents himself for a further period of six months. Would he be eligible to receive the pension during the second consecutive six-months period or the one or two-months period, or is it for one period only?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No; he could repeat.
There is no limit to the number of times that he can be absent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am informed that this could be done.

So presumably a person could be absent within a few days of the calendar year and still continue to receive his pension outside the country for the whole year or practically the whole year, and keep this up indefinitely?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: This is so, Mr. Chairman, but it is felt, of course, that a person is not going to be moving back and taking up residence in Canada every six months and continue that sort of thing.

I would submit that this could be done very easily if the person happens to live in the United States or wants to move or has moved to the United States, or originally came from the United States and has relatives there who live fairly close to the border. This would be establishing a silly situation, or a discriminatory situation because we are saying to those people who live in the United States from which it is easy to return to Canada that they are in a class different from those who move to the United Kingdom for a six months period or longer if they want to live there permanently. If they are not able to take advantage of the provision of the legislation in the same way as a person who moves to the United States might be, it is discrimination. I couple this with the thoughts that I have expressed about the need to make it universally applicable. While there may be some complications in this regard in so far 79951-0-2881
Old Age Security Act
as the rules are concerned, nevertheless I should like to have this appear on the record in a clear way. Perhaps, therefore, Mr. Chairman, an amendment is in order. I move:
That the proposed new subsection (1) of section 5 in clause 1 of the bill be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"(1) Where a pensioner absents himself from Canada payment of his pension for any period he continues to be absent from Canada shall be continued unless the pension is otherwise suspended or voided pursuant to the provisions of this act".

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
That the standing committee on agriculture and colonization be empowered to inquire into the prices of farm machinery and to report to the house thereon.
He said: Mr. Speaker, during the past 10 years the most frequently heard general complaint on the part of farmers has been over the cost-price squeeze. This arises from the fact that during this period the prices received by farmers for their products either have not increased or have not increased in anything like the proportion of the increase in cost of the goods and services farmers have to purchase.
One of the big items in a farmer's costs is the cost of machinery and the cost of repairs to keep the machinery in operation. There has been a great deal of dissatisfaction on the part of farmers about the increase that has occurred in the cost of farm machinery. One seldom attends a meeting of farmers without hearing instances cited of the comparative costs of tractors or combines 10 or 12 years ago and today with various figures being adduced to show that the cost has increased two or three times over what it was in the previous period.
In view of the desirability of bringing down the costs to farmers and particularly of preventing further increases in cost of the things they have to buy I feel that an inquiry into the reasons why the costs of farm machinery have increased as they have would be in the public interest. I would hope that this inquiry would enable the committee not only to determine the reasons why this increase in cost has occurred but also to make recommendations as to how further increases
Agriculture Committee
could be prevented or how present prices could be turned down a bit or reduced.
There are a number of facets to the whole question which I think could be profitably studied. One way in which costs have been held down and have not increased at the rate at which they otherwise might have has been because of standardization and I believe much more could be accomplished by way of standardization in the manufacture of farm machinery. I have received a considerable number of suggestions from farmers saying that the standardization of nuts and bolts alone on farm machinery would save them a great deal of time and money. Each machine they buy requires nuts and bolts of a different size and type. If one of these breaks they often have difficulty obtaining the proper type to replace it. Greater standardization would save a considerable sum of money in repairs and the saving of time in the period of harvesting or seeding would be substantial and perhaps of even more importance. Any time lost by farmers in those periods represents a financial loss.
That is only one phase of the matter. In addition, I think more could be done by way of standardization from the point of view that instead of there being a considerable number of large heavy separate machines, one for each operation which has to be carried on in farming, there could be two or three basic machines and through the use of simplified and cheaper attachments it would be possible to carry on the work that now requires several large expensive and heavy machines.
This is a large subject for inquiry, of course. I would not anticipate that the committee would be able to complete its study in the remainder of this session. I would hope, however, that it could make a good start on the inquiry this year, lay out the general lines it will develop, hear some evidence in connection with the matter and then be in a position to proceed with an investigation at the next session and complete the inquiry and report.
It is my hope that the motion will be passed expeditiously and that the committee could immediately start to work on this inquiry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any effort that will assist the farmers of Canada in meeting the economic problems that confront them will win wide support, I am sure, in every quarter of the house. There can be no doubt that agriculture today is faced with a critical situation as we have had occasion to remind the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) from time to time.

Agriculture Committee The cost-price squeeze is still a fact notwithstanding the statement made by the minister a few months ago to the effect that the government had resolved this problem. The fact is that the cost-price squeeze now is as great as ever.
Undoubtedly, one of the considerations the government had in mind in bringing forward this proposal was, I am sure, the desire to examine the cost of agricultural machinery but also to remove an embarrassment which doubtlessly confronts the Minister of Agri-cuture and the government at every step. The government, I have no doubt, particularly from the words which have just been used by the minister, namely that the study is not one that need be terminated now, indicates that what the minister has in mind is what will be the situation when the next federal election comes and when the farmers will be confronting the minister with the fact that the cost-price squeeze still exists.
I have no doubt that with the great imaginative powers that are his the minister is now anticipating that situation and he will be in a position to say to the farmers, "Oh, but we have done something about this; we have established a committee to look into the matter of the high cost of farm machinery; this was done by us; this was an indication of our concern about the fact that farmers operate under difficult conditions". Farm prices are down; the cost of necessities are up. That is undoubtedly what the minister had in mind-

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member it was not.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
-although the minister did not say that. In any event, it is so obvious that such is the case that I should not be given any credit for reading this motive into the words of the minister.
The fact is that agriculture is now confronted with critical situations. This is admitted on all sides. The economic return of many thousands of farmers in this country at this time is such that it should be the concern of governments on all levels to ascertain, both by way of fundamental action and by way of what might be characterized as temporary remedial action, as to how to deal with this situation.
It will be recalled that the previous administration took the iniative of abolishing the tariffs on farm machinery thereby very considerably bringing farm machinery within the reach of many thousands of farmers who otherwise would not have been able to provide themselves with the necessary equipment. This study will be welcomed as a means of confirming the decision of the previous administration to reduce tariff rates


on farm implements completely; but the minister should be warned that this study, desirable as it is, will not be regarded as satisfying the obligations of the government in terms of an agricultural policy which it assured the Canadian people it would give them, a policy that would improve the economic situation of agriculture at this time.
The minister mentioned the fact that consideration and study should be given to the standardization of equipment. We will have to look at that in the light of the fact that we recognize the private sector of our economy is something that we wish to encourage. That should not deter us from making an examination of the problem from every point of view. There is also the constitutional aspect as to whether or not a committee of this house has the power to recommend standardization. It will be doubtful that it has the power to take any steps pursuant to the results of a positive study on the question of standardization. But I have no doubt that a study along those lines will prove constructive and valuable.
Those of us who represent agricultural constituencies in part know many farmers who are loaded with equipment beyond their means. Of that there can be no doubt. I have in my own mind as I talk right now some cases of individuals who find themselves economically embarrassed because of the heavy overhead which they have had imposed on them. When I say "which they have had imposed on them" I use the words deliberately. So, to the extent that this will reveal a situation which disturbs farmers and should disturb us we welcome this proposal. But I say to the minister that this looks too much like an effort on his part to divert the charge that he has not dealt with the cost-price squeeze situation along the lines indicated by him and by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and those who have been spokesmen for the government.
We shall do our part in seeing that this study is complete, that it is vigorously pursued, but we shall also be vigorous in our examination of other aspects of the government's agricultural policy which more and more gives evidence of being wanting.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this group agrees with the purpose of the resolution. We think it is a very necessary inquiry. We also think it is very late in the session to introduce a resolution and to refer such an important matter to the committee on agriculture. We are of the opinion that this resolution should have come before the house in January so that the committee would have had full opportunity to

study all aspects of this question, and there are a lot of aspects to be probed.
I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Essex East (Mr Martin) that while this is a very important matter, the question of how costs are affected by the rising price of farm machinery, the farmers are also interested in hearing of government action with respect to prices and improvements in that regard.
1 am inclined to think that this is rather a diversionary tactic, you know, to take the attention of the farmer away from the main things that concern him at the present time and focus it on one segment of his present problems. There is no doubt about this inquiry being necessary. As I look over the latest return from the dominion bureau of statistics, which I received recently, I find it shows that while the index of some agricultural costs dropped in recent months, the index of equipment and material advanced 1.4 per cent since January, from 218.8 to 221.9.
The minister informed us that the committee was to be instructed to inquire into the reasons for the increase in the cost of farm machinery. That is a very good purpose, and it will have power to make recommendations to prevent further increases or stabilize the present costs of farm machinery. We agree with that.
There are a number of important aspects of the cost of farm machinery to which the committee could give some careful attention. That will require considerable time. The minister has implied that the committee could not finish its work this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext: I did not imply it; I said definitely it would not.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
I did not hear quite correctly. Some of the members opposite me were talking and I could not hear too well. I must always lay the blame on the Conservative members opposite. I think it far better to take time to make a full report than to hurry through in a few short weeks time and make an early and incomplete report.
The minister mentioned the standardization of parts, bolts and nuts. I think that is a very important suggestion. Anyone who has had anything to do with farm machinery knows what time can be lost, what expenses can be incurred in this way. I know from my own experience in the interior of British Columbia and from the experience of other persons working in our district that this lack of standardization makes it necessary sometimes to wire to Vancouver for a special size of bolt and nut and things of that sort. It is very important. I think that some study
Agriculture Committee should be made with respect to the standardization to a greater extent of types of farm machinery, manufactured types of machinery for purposes on the farm. There could be greater standardization of the types of machinery as well as the parts of machinery.
I was interested in the minister's suggestion with respect to basic machines. I think there is a lot in his suggestion. In my opinion a great deal of duplication of expense is caused to farmers today by farmers owning expensive machinery when with proper arrangements there could be cooperative ownership of certain basic machines. That is particularly so in the case of land clearing, draining, diking and things of that sort. In those fields there is an opportunity for co-operative ownership of large basic machines to the advantage of farmers within an area. Thus farmers could reduce to some extent their capital investment in machinery which is becoming so large that more and more land is being required to carry the load.
I think there should also be an examination into how sales charges affect the cost of farm machinery. While the dealer has to have adequate remuneration, I think there is some duplication in respect of distribution which adds to the cost of machinery. When you have a certain limited market it is all right to talk about the spirit of competition but there is very little competition with regard to the price charged for a tractor, a binder or a mowing machine of a certain type as between one company and another. I have noticed that where outlets are limited you will find two or three engaged in the distribution of farm machinery and I think something should be done by the companies themselves to reduce the cost of distribution and sales charges by some consideration of that aspect of the problem.
I think the committee should also inquire into the application of the tariff structure with respect to the admission of farm implements into Canada free of duty. In my own personal experience since I have been a member of the house I have on various occasions had poultry producers and fruit farmers come to me and say that certain parts they required for their equipment were not duty free, and after considerable representations being made to the minister the matter was corrected in one or two cases. But I do suggest that the committee should have officials of the Department of National Revenue come before it in order to get their views as to what is considered to be agricultural equipment.
I remember that on one occasion some parts were required for a particular type of incubator and the customs officials said that

Agriculture Committee according to the act an incubator was not an agricultural machine. Yet it certainly is a piece of machinery used for the production of chickens which is a part of agriculture, and after some time I think an amendment was finally made to the regulations and these parts were admitted. There may be other cases like that and I suggest that the committee should have officials of the Department of National Revenue come before it and explain what actually is allowed into Canada under the term "agricultural implement", shall I say.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext: It would be interesting to know why this matter was brought forward in the month of June, so late.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
I do not think the officials of the Department of National Revenue would be able to answer that question but it might be a good idea to have the minister come before the committee in order to find out the reasons for the delay in bringing in this resolution.
I think there should also be some consideration of the cost of transportation of farm machinery. This is also related to the matter of the outlets for distribution. I think some savings possibly could be made by more scientific and economical loading of equipment from eastern factories destined to western points so that the costs could be reduced as far as possible by following the most economic route and moving the machinery to the centre most easily available to the farmer who may be making the purchase.
I have dealt with these matters because they have been brought to my attention throughout the years. This group wholeheartedly supports the purpose of the resolution. We hope the committee will make a thorough study of the question while they are at it even though it will extend into the next session and that the work of the committee will result in a lowering or stabilization of the cost of farm machinery and to that extent be of benefit to the farmers.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and the government for this important step. I have been hoping for some time that such a resolution would be introduced by the government and I am very glad indeed that the minister is bringing it in now. This is one of the problems that the government inherited when it took office. Despite what the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) has said, there are a lot of people in western Canada who are interested in the price of farm machinery and who feel that the former government did

not do a great deal over the years when he was sitting on the treasury benches. We are all very glad to note that now he is in the opposition he has developed an interest in the prices of farm machinery.
This matter is of particular interest to the farmers of Saskatchewan and western Canada generally. The cost-price squeeze is something we have heard a great deal about in recent years. Tractors and combines that used to cost from $2,000 to $3,000 now cost between $6,000 and $7,000. Other farm machinery is on the same level. The price of repairs is out of all proportion to the money received by the farmers for their produce. Therefore the farmers are all interested in this matter. I am glad the minister has intimated that the committee is going to have wide powers. I hope it will be entitled to inquire into the prices charged and the profits being made by the machinery companies. There is a general feeling throughout western Canada that they are making tremendous profits. I have my doubts whether that is so but I think it would be advisable for the committee to have full power to inquire into that matter, to inquire into the cost of their raw materials and find out what has made it necessary for the price of farm equipment to be increased so much.
I shall only be about two minutes, Mr. Speaker. I hope that all these matters will be gone into by the committee. The minister has intimated that it will have power to sit after the session is over and that it will be a continuing committee to investigate all these various matters that are of interest to the people of western Canada. As a result of the deliberations of the committee and the recommendations that are made, I hope the prices of farm machinery will be brought more into line with the prices of the products that the farmers have to sell.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to compliment the minister for having taken the action he is taking in setting up this particular committee. It is one that I am quite sure all of the farmers in eastern Canada in particular will appreciate. However, we deplore the fact that it should be set up as late in the session as it is being set up. It is unfortunate that committees in the House of Commons do not function between sessions. If we are going to make a real success of this

particular committee and if it is to accomplish what I am quite sure the farmers, the minister and other segments of the economy are interested in having it do, it would seem to me that it is going to have to go fairly extensively into the whole field of machinery costing and pricing.
I should like to see labour called before this particular committee because continually the charge is made to the farmer by the machine distributor, the machine manufacturing industry and politicians also that the reason farm machinery is at such a high price and that the cost to the farmer is so high is that labour is getting too much of the machinery dollar. I should like to see called before the committee representatives of the farm machinery industry-particularly the management side of it; labour representatives; representatives of the unions; the distributor representatives and the retail merchants themselves. I think we shall find in Canada a situation similar to that found in the United States about 10 years ago or a little more when an investigation was conducted there into farm machinery.
In Ontario one of the problems affecting the machine industry that I think should be investigated is the retail price of or the cost involved in secondhand machinery itself. When a farmer can no longer use the machinery he has and he is obliged to trade it in on something new, the amount received for the equipment is not in keeping with the amount of money that he has had to pay for it. Yet somebody buying that machinery for the second time finds there is not a great deal of saving in it.
I am thinking mainly of the milk-producing industry in Ontario in the last few years where they have changed over from farmers who are operating with milking machines and modern cooling equipment that went along with the milking machine in dairy production. All of a sudden in southern Ontario-it is into this matter that part of the investigation might take place-there seemed to be a terrific impetus for bulk haulage. Bulk haulage not only meant that the milk was going to be hauled in bulk trucks but that the farmer had to have bulk coolers and the equipment all had to be changed over. The cost was phenomenal. At the same time the farmers in those areas that were not going into bulk haulage found that the cost of cooling equipment for the old type of milk set-up was a very expensive proposition even when they were buying secondhand.
It would also appear that some investigation can take place, particularly in the east, in relation to patents that are held on an
Agriculture Committee international basis. I am referring to equipment that has been manufactured and that appears to have been very much cheaper than former farm equipment that is held under international patents, and where this equipment has only been available from one major company. It would seem to me that this situation has caused other companies to go into producing costly equipment that has in many cases been an experiment tried out on the farmer, at the farmer's own cost; and that after he has used the new invention for a short time he finds it has been replaced by something that has been further developed and is much more satisfactory than the other property.
This investigation also, I would think, should give close consideration to the price of farm machinery replacement costs. In Ontario, and particularly in northern Ontario, parts are not stocked in the main at any place in the area. If you have a major breakdown the distributors, or the small distributors anyway, have not parts for a great deal of major machinery. There is not the same requirement that there is with regard to automobiles where you must in Canada for a number of years by law stock parts for this equipment. But it often seems that the part you need for such things as discs and plows and other articles of farm machinery that will last a much longer time than normal farm equipment are not available anywhere in Canada and it takes months to get them. It is wise to order parts in the fall so that you will have them in time for spring. When these parts come the cost has no relationship to the normal cost of parts but they would appear to have been made especially for a custom job.
As I understand the situation with automobile parts, the automobile supplier is by law compelled to keep the equipment for manufacturing parts for a particular model for a certain length of time after the particular year. Parts should be available, I think, by law, for a period of 10 years or something of that nature. Some consideration could be given to that problem with regard to agricultural machinery repairs also.
I think the minister is quite right in saying that a great deal of advantage can be gained from the farmers deciding on a basic type of equipment and having that type developed. But I would be greatly interested in knowing just how the minister expects there is going to be this basic type development. I am quite sure we will all agree that there are basic units that could be modified and added to and one of them, of course, is the Ferguson set-up. But I would suggest that we are going to have a great deal of

Agriculture Committee difficulty in getting all the companies to accept this basic type of equipment and to limit the manufacturing of those that wish to manufacture other things. As long as there is competition I would assume that the price is going to have to go up, that distribution costs are going to increase as well as advertising costs and all the others costs. I agree with the minister that if standardization of basic units could be accomplished it would reduce the price of farm equipment considerably.
This statement also would be true with regard to automobiles in Canada and a great number of other things. A basic unit could be produced for a very reasonable sum of money. But we have not yet found any method of persuading companies to produce according to our needs and desires. Rather they produce to satisfy the market in which they can sell their particular product.
I believe the various segments of the industry should be given an opportunity to appear here. Not only should they be given the opportunity but they should be instructed to appear before the committee. Time is limited. I would suggest that we should have this investigation completed before too long, either this session or early next session, because we know and realize the fear the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) expressed, that we will be facing an election and that this will be a promise in the election platform rather than an actual fact.
I am pleased that the minister has now seen fit to do something with the agricultural committee which I think is constructive and which is very basic. I hope that the committee will be givan all the authority it needs in order to get a true picture so that parliament itself can decide who is the fly in the ointment. When they decide who is the fly in the ointment they can do something about the problem.
Mr, C. S. Smallwood (Battle River-
Camrose): Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes of the house's time to answer a couple of charges which have been made by members of the opposition that this is an election issue.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) suggested that the farmers should buy co-operatively. For his benefit, let me tell him that every farmer needs his own machinery. I have an expensive combine, and last year I had three days of fine weather to take off my crops. If four or five farmers together bought that piece of machinery, what could they do with it on an occasion like that? The previous year we had four days of good weather, so suggestions like that seem to me to be ridiculous.


I always like to listen to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) speak on agriculture because he can rant around and always turn it into a political speech. May I say that when I speak of agriculture I have had experience. I would say I have had twenty years more experience than the hon. member for Essex East has had, or perhaps I should say 19 years and 364 days. I have before me an editorial from the Ottawa Journal of February 17, 1960 which reads, in part, as follows:
Political piglet gives Paul rough time.
He was speaking in Kingston, Ontario, so I will give the hon. member credit for one day's farm experience that week.
I would also like to draw the attention of this committee to the fact that on April 23, 1959, at page 2985 of Hansard, I drew the attention of the house to the situation with regard to the price of machinery. On page 2991 of Hansard for the same year the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) drew the attention of the house to the price of machinery. If we look back to the year 1953 when the Liberals were in power, did they do anything to help us out of the squeeze we were in? Absolutely nothing. The only thing I can remember their doing was at a meeting in Manitoba when one of the farmers got up and asked the Right Hon. C. D. Howe "How about the price of oats?", and he poked the farmer in the stomach and said, "You look well fed". That is the kind of support we had from those gentlemen. This government has been interested in the price of machinery and the welfare of the farmer, ever since elected. This matter is no election issue because this question has been brought to the attention of the minister by the farmer members of this party.
