speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this motion, first because it was in the committee where the subject was raised. Since I was the one who suggested it I feel that I should stand at this time and tell the opposition the reason why it was suggested.
There was no thought in my mind of political motives; I can assure the hon. members opposite of that. It was out of a feeling which comes from having lived in close association with farmers in western Canada and of being a farmer myself. Let me say that the agriculture committee when it has made the study and completed its deliberations will report back to the house. In the meetings of the standing committee on agriculture and colonization, which is made up of a cross section of all people in all parties in this house, each member of the committee will have full opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses which appear before the committee.
I see no political implications in this whatsoever. The purpose behind this suggestion contained no thought on my part of any persecution of any machine companies. It was simply to provide an opportunity of which advantage can be taken to study the price of farm machinery. It will be the function of the committee to call witnesses before it and to examine the facts; in other words, to get the facts clarified and get them on the table so that they can be examined. Let everyone who can make a contribution to the solution of this problem do so when the matter is before the committee.
As one moves among the farmers of western Canada he finds there is no problem which occupies more attention or causes more discussion than the cost of farm machinery. I am told that the costs of some machines have risen by 200, or even 300 per cent. If this committee wants to find out what are the reasons behind this startling rise in the cost of machinery, let it devote its best efforts to the task. The farmer is faced with the problem of costs on one hand and the price of his commodity on the other. He is caught in the squeeze which is known as the cost-price squeeze. His net income is shrinking year after year. It is to examine this question, to go back behind costs and prices in order to

Agriculture Committee see what can be done to give the farmer a square deal-that is the end result hoped for in this study of farm machinery prices.
I want to say in closing how grateful everyone in this house should be for the forwardthinking and considered motives of the government and of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) in permitting this resolution to come before the house. It is a constructive proposal. It is one for which the farm people are asking. It is a subject upon which letters reach me every day. Perhaps this is because in my constituency of Macleod in southwestern Alberta I happen to be a farmer as well as an economist; perhaps it is because one third of the wheat in the province of Alberta is grown in my constituency. Little wonder I rise at this time to say what I have said concerning the need of a thorough and far-reaching investigation into the price of farm machinery as it affects the net income of farmers.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
No one can
dispute that I am a farmer. That is one thing. Another thing is that no one can say: "I was born ten years before you", because I certainly am no chicken. I have been through all the stages of farming. I came into the Peace river country very early on. We had four horses and four bottom plough, also a breaking plough but we came to the point where we did not know whether we owned the place or whether the machinery company owned it.
That is what is wrong today. The cost of machinery is too high. The cost of repairs is too high. The farmer out west does not want to milk cows. He wants to buy milk at the store or he wants to buy his margarine at the store. He does not buy butter. That is one of the things that is wrong with farming. When we were on the farm we milked a slew of cows every night. We worked the horses long hours. Now a young fellow wants to work ten or 12 hours on a tractor costing $10,000. The tractors have to be large; they have to draw five ploughs instead of the old-time gang plough. They have to be diesel, and everything has to be done in a hurry. That is another of the things that is wrong with farming.
Then again, the cost of machinery repairs is too high. Why that should be, I do not know. That is what this committee is going to do. We are going to find out why.
We know that farming is in a dire situation. In the Peace river country we are getting by. We are growing grass seeds. We have a market in Europe, and we sell all kinds of grass seed. We are even growing blue grass seed. As long as there is a good market, you are all right. Again, we

grow lots of barley there, and our wheat is doing fine. The wheat was up, probably three weeks ago, then we had a snow storm. We had two feet of snow there. But that does not hurt the wheat, though it would probably affect oats and barley.
We have to find out where the farmers' extra money is going. A farmer makes $7,000, $8,000 or $10,000 a year, yet he probably has nothing after he has paid off his creditors. He is broke and has to start right back in again. It is the greatest "next year country" you ever saw, especially the country where we live. Always next year. But it is a great country, and one of the best.
We shall make out all right. We are Canadians. We have always made out and if this committee can just help us a little we shall do just fine.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
Hearing the remarks of the previous speaker reminded me of one of my favourite House of Commons stories. The comment I have in mind was made by a former Liberal member from Saskatchewan by the name of Studer. He was speaking of how long he had lived on the prairies, and he went on to say that unfortunately he and his dad had not started in a sod hut in the way so many people who had gone to the prairies had done. "We did not start in a sod hut" he added, "but once dad made a little bit we sure moved into one fast".
I mention this story in a sense as an excuse for speaking on this occasion. I have not much agriculture in my constituency, and if the present trend continues we are going to have even less. However, there are several points in connection with the operations of the committee that I should like to bring to the attention of the house. I think we all recognize that this kind of investigation is likely to require considerable statistical analysis and a great deal of economic figuring. I have not heard from the minister whether he believes that this committee should be provided with economic assistance; I mean, the assistance of economists and also of some kind of counsel to arrange for appearances and that type of thing. My experience is that committees of this house in the main are not equipped to carry on an investigation, especially from one session to another, on a topic as complex as this without any type of economic advice. I think the best thing the committee could do would be to search around and find a good agricultural economist to be its guide in the analysis, especially, of company reports.
I have in my hand a pamphlet put out by the Canadian Labour Congress called: "The

real story behind the rise of prices of farm machinery". This was published in 1958 and the figures contained in it were taken from the dominion bureau of statistics. I want to outline what this pamphlet seeks to put over in order to make the point that economic analysis is going to be very important in getting to the root of this problem. The pamphlet starts by saying that prices rose 94 per cent in the 12-year period between 1945 and 1957.
It makes the point, again from statistical analysis, that workers' earnings were up 108 per cent but the total number of workers required in the agricultural implement industry in Canada was down 31 per cent; that the total wage bill was up 43 per cent-there are statistics and charts to support it-that the total gross production was up 113 per cent; the net value was up 93 per cent; the production per worker was up 180 per cent but the wage share of sales was down. In 1945 wages made up almost 65 per cent of the net value of agricultural implement production and in 1957 the percentage had fallen to 48. The pamphlet goes on to ask how a fall in wage costs can cause a rise in prices. In my opinion this kind of analysis will have to be made of the agricultural industry before any conclusions can be reached.
In the last hour or so I checked the indexes of Hansard over the years to discover how much interest had been shown in this topic in the house. Going back to 1952 I was surprised to find that the topic was not raised very frequently. It was raised occasionally by Social Credit members from Alberta and by C.C.F. members from Saskatchewan but it has not been a topic of much concern since 1952. At that time there was considerable interest because of the investigation that had taken place in Saskatchewan. I propose to read from Hansard of April 22, 1952 at page 1487. Mr. M. J. Coldwell speaking on that occasion said:
I wanted to say something about farm implement prices. I have just examined a copy of the final report submitted by the Saskatchewan legislative committee on farm implements and passed unanimously by the legislative assembly of that province on April 4. This committee was appointed to inquire into the prices of farm machinery with the object of determining the possibility of establishing parity in prices between farm machinery and the prices of farm products.
Its significance can be determined when one considers the importance of machinery to those engaged in modern mechanized agriculture. The trend toward mechanized farming, not only in Saskatchewan and the prairie provinces but indeed all across Canada, has progressed with great rapidity over the years with the result that farm implements are more important than ever to the farmer. Yet despite the importance of this subject to a large section of our economy the committee reports that the four major companies of the farm implement industry, namely, John Deere, International
Agriculture Committee Harvester, Cockshutt and Massey-Harris, failed to provide the committee with the necessary information to carry out its inquiry. However, this did not prevent the committee from obtaining evidence which clearly indicated high prices and resulting high profits in that industry.
The Saskatchewan committee recommended that in view of the failure of the above companies to comply with the committee's request for information and in view of evidence submitted indicating very high prices and profits the federal government be urged to immediately institute an investigation of the farm implement industry by a parliamentary committee. Despite the Liberal party's great love for the farmers and the wonderful deeds it performed for them it never got around to following up that recommendation and establishing a parliamentary committee. Mr. Cold-well went on to point out that the parliamentary committee established in 1937 brought out a report similar to that brought out by the Saskatchewan committee. It, too, was very critical of the machinery manufacturers.
The present committee has a real job on its hands. I am pleased that it is going to tackle the problem even though it is late in the session. The establishment of the committee indicates that the minister is listening to some of the backbenchers from the west. From talking to them I know it is a major concern of theirs. I hope the minister will do his best along with the committee to encourage the work of the committee on a basis that has expert advice.
In launching a study of this nature, as the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said, you have to take into account the union relationship. I know there is a strong feeling on this question in the united automobile workers which is the union that happened to organize most of the farm machinery plants. They would like an opportunity to present and prove the case-they think they can do it-that it is not the wage part of the costs of machinery that has sent prices skyrocketing to the extent they have. I know they will welcome an opportunity to cooperate with the committee in its study.
Before taking my seat I want to rebut the hon. member who suggested that the salaries of union officials have contributed to the increase of farm machinery costs. I think the hon. gentleman should be fair to union officials and recognize that they are not on the payroll of any of the companies. Their pay comes from fees paid by members of the union. As far as I know membership fees have never been a part of the contribution management makes. That is the contribution the employee makes-

speechtext:
Yes, out of his wages.

Agriculture Committee

speechtext: Mr Speaker, I was going to say something about the setting up of the committee but since there is such unanimity on all sides of the house may I respectfully desist from saying anything in the hope that perhaps the motion could be put.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO FARM MACHINERY PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I trust the minister's wishes will be met eventually as they are on all matters. It is regrettable that a motion of this importance should have been introduced in what some hon. members opposite like to think are the dying weeks of this session. It follows the pattern established by the government of holding up matters of importance until the last moment. It would have assisted the farmers and members of the committee if the matter had been brought forward early in the year.
In the past five or six years there has been a 6 per cent increase in farm implement prices, as those qualified to speak about agriculture will verify, with no relationship to the wages paid in that industry. Wage increases have not kept pace with increases in the price of machinery.
About two years ago farm machinery prices increased by 6 per cent across the board coincidentally with the dollar an acre payment made to the farmers from the federal treasury. Farm people tend to attach the blame for high farm machinery prices to the wages paid to the workers in that industry. I know, too- not having a farming background but an industrial field background-that I can look back to the time when industrial workers were of the opinion that the main reason farm products were high priced and increasing in price was that the farmer spent six months of the year in California or in Florida. We know how ridiculous that is, but this attitude existed and this feeling was developed by those who apparently did not want the industrial workers to know the facts but wanted to leave the impression with them that the farmer was at fault in so far as the cost of his products was concerned. I am not getting away from the subject matter under discussion, Mr. Speaker, but I did want to make a comparison between the two industries and the attitude that existed at that time.
In 1936 or 1937 a committee of this house studied substantially the same question and came to some conclusions about farm machinery prices. This may be good background information for the members of the committee

when they study this particular subject. I should like to give one brief quotation from page 18 of the report of the committee, which reads as follows:
The committee concludes, therefore, that there is competition in the matter of securing sales, but little or no effective competition in the matter of prices as between companies. In January, 1936, and throughout the period, increases in the price or maintenance of prices when a decrease should have been expected occurred simultaneously in all the companies.
There is one reference to the fact that there is a fairly co-operative spirit and there was a fairly co-operative spirit among farm implement machinery companies some 25 years ago. The same thought exists at the moment. I have the 1958 report of Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited. This is a report made directly to the annual meeting. In this report reference is made also to price agreements and price collusion and that there was no price competition between farm implement companies in the sale of their products or of their machinery and equipment. I do not wish to read the whole report but merely to refer to this reference to show that this is part of the annual report. As the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) pointed out

I think this is a valid suggestion and is one which should have been given consideration before-what affects farm machinery prices, what causes them to rise, takes in the whole field of profits, wages, transportation costs, distribution costs, production costs, productivity, all sorts of other similar factors.
Most committees of the house have some difficulty in dealing with complex problems of this nature and operate on a sort of scatter-gun basis. This is no reflection on the members of this house or of the committee; it is just unfortunate because of the other work that members have to do, because of the lack of research facilities and assistance available to them. Because of this most members of the committee find it extremely difficult to go too deeply and thoroughly into any such subject as this which involves all of those complex and interrelated factors. In order for this committee, even at this late date of the session, to do an effective job in analysing and carrying out the responsibilities which this house is about to give to it, it should have attached to it a research staff on agriculture consisting of agricultural economists and someone in that field who is able to counsel the committee and study and prepare material for the committee to come to grips with the problem. Without such research facilities and research staff being made available to the committee I am of the

opinion that it will be relatively ineffective in getting to the root of the particular problem itself.
Because there is a short time between now and the end of the session I would rather expect that this house should also give authority to this committee to function, to meet, travel and study this question in the time between this session and the next session of parliament in order that they may make an unhurried approach to this problem and, with the research staff that they should have at their disposal, be able to make as thorough a study as possible of this particular question.
I also think that the committee should have complete and ready access to all of the information and files of the combines investigation branch which periodically over the years has dealt with and followed up the question of farm machinery prices. If these three things are done, Mr. Speaker, we will have an opportunity to do something about this matter and we shall have every hope to expect from the committee a report that will indicate a thorough study in depth and an analysis and be able to make recommendations based on a thorough study of the problem and what should be done to overcome it.
I reiterate the three points. I think the committee should have attached to it a staff of research men, statisticians, economists; people of that nature who would work with it and counsel it. I think it should have authority to meet between now and the next session and during the next session also, if necessary; it should have the authority to travel and to study this question as thoroughly as possible. I think it should also have complete access to the files of the combines investigation branch, as well as being given the opportunity to hear every last possible person, union, corporation, and otherwise who wishes to appear before the committee to present their arguments and their cases.

Mr. Speaker, I was very glad to learn that this motion has received strong support from every part of the house. They appear to be strongly in favour of the setting up of the committee but still they want to strongly criticize it.
Agriculture Committee
I must say I was disappointed in the line taken by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), followed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and to some extent by members of the C.C.F., in which they imputed to me entirely political motives in setting up this committee. While I was disappointed in their taking that line I must say, Mr. Speaker, I was not a bit surprised because some people's minds run only in one groove and they just cannot get out of it. However, I can assure, Mr. Speaker, and through you, hon. members opposite, that their ever present suspicions along those lines are followed by their own thoughts along that line and have no foundation in fact so far as I am concerned in connnection with this particular matter.
As far as the procedure followed by the committee is concerned, hon. members here are aware that the procedure in each committee is in its own hands; it makes its own decisions in regard to how the inquiry it is engaged in will be carried on, and I have no doubt that that procedure will be followed in so far as this committee on agriculture is concerned. In this particular case the committee has the full powers of any other committee to send for persons, papers, and so on.
Some question was raised by hon. members opposite and criticism voiced over the fact that the committee is being given this particular inquiry to carry out at this particular time in the session. The answer to that is very simple indeed. The agriculture comittee has been occupied up to this time with an inquiry into the milling of feed grains and the marketing of such grains in western Canada. That was an urgent matter requiring investigation and the committee has been quite fully occupied with that field of inquiry. But now that that inquiry has drawn to a close the committee is being given this subject matter for investigation by them.
I was rather interested in seeing that all of the members of the C.C.F. party present seemed to think it was necessary to speak in support of the motion and they also seemed to think it was necessary in a way to put up a defence of the labour cost factor in farm implements. Resolved, that is it expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:
(1)	That the increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the deduction from tax granted to taxpayers in a province which imposes an income tax on individuals be continued for the 1960 and 1961 taxation years.
(2)	That for the 1960 and 1961 taxation years the deduction from tax allowed to corporations in respect of income earned in a province which imposes an income tax on corporations and in which arrangements exist for the replacement of federal grants to universities by additional provincial grants in accordance with the proposed amendments to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act be increased from 9 per cent to 10 per cent in respect of income earned after December 31, 1959.
(3)	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years the maximum amount deductible from income on account of medical expenses be increased to $3000 for taxpayers who are entitled to claim the deduction for married status and $2500 for other taxpayers (not exceeding $3000 for husband and wife together) plus $750 in respect of each dependant of the taxpayer up to a maximum of $3000 in respect of dependants.
(4)	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years, where a person who formerly carried on a business in Canada the income from which was

computed by the cash method has ceased to be a resident of Canada, there shall be included in computing his income from the business for the last year in which he resided in Canada the value of the accounts receivable and inventory at the time he ceased to reside in Canada.
(5)	That with respect to any amalgamation after March 31, 1960 any share other than a common share of a new corporation resulting from an amalgamation shall be deemed to be a liability of the new corporation for purposes of section 105C of the act.
(6)	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years no deduction shall be made as an allowance in respect of an oil or gas well or a mine in computing the income of a non-resident-owned investment corporation.
(7)	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years, for purposes of calculating the amount of the credit a taxpayer may claim in respect of taxes paid to a foreign country, the limitation at present computed by reference to the tax paid to the foreign country on that part of his income from sources in the foreign country that is also subject to tax in Canada be amended so as to be computed by reference to the income tax (other than income tax on dividends which are deductible by the taxpayer) paid to the foreign country.
(8)	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years the rules for determining income from a source be amended to specify the deductions that shall be made in computing the income of a nonresident person from a business or employment in Canada and in computing income from sources outside Canada for the purpose of calculating the foreign tax credit allowed to a person resident in Canada.
(9)	That for the 1961 and subsequent taxation years for purposes of the provision that only one of a group of associated corporations shall receive the benefit of the lower rate of tax on the first $25,000 of taxable income the present rule for determining whether one corporation is associated with another, which is based on ownership of shares, be replaced by a rule related to control of the corporations.
(10)	That the four-year period, after which the minister may not make a re-assessment of the tax payable for a taxation year unless there has been fraud or misrepresentation by the taxpayer or the person filing the return, shall commence with the date of mailing by the minister to the taxpayer of the original assessment or of a notification that no tax was payable for the year.
(11)	That the four-year time limit, after which the minister may not make a re-assessment unless there has been fraud or misrepresentation by the taxpayer or person filing the return, may be waived by the taxpayer by notice to the minister.
(12)	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years a corporation whose principal business is production or marketing of sodium chloride or whose business includes extraction of sodium chloride from halite deposits may deduct in computing its income drilling and exploration expenses incurred by it in the year in exploring or drilling for halite.
(13)	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years an individual who receives a superannuation,

pension or death benefit or a benefit under a registered retirement savings plan in respect of which any tax under the Estate Tax Act or succession duty imposed by a province was payable in respect of a death occurring after December 31, 1958 may deduct in computing his income for the year a portion of the benefit received by him determined by reference to the tax or duty applicable to the benefit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

That is correct. The committee will appreciate that non-resident-owned investment corporations are Canadian companies all of whose income is from investments and 95 per cent of whose shares are owned by non-residents. Such companies are taxed at a rate of 15 per cent. When such companies pay dividends to their non-resident shareholders no non-resident tax is withheld. In other words, the 15 per cent tax paid by the non-resident-owned investment corporation is in lieu of the 15 per cent tax which non-residents would have to pay if they derived dividends or interest directly from Canadian sources.
As the law stands at present a non-resident-owned investment corporation may deduct a depletion allowance in respect of dividends it receives from Canadian oil, gas or mining companies before paying its 15 per cent tax. If a non-resident received dividends directly from Canadian oil, gas or mining companies instead of through an N.R.O. he would not be entitled to any depletion allowance. This amendment is intended to withdraw this unintended advantage now available to those who receive oil, gas or mining company dividends indirectly through an N.R.O.
Accordingly this paragraph would place dividends from Canadian mining, oil or gas companies received by a non-resident through a non-resident-owned investment corporation on the same basis for tax purposes as dividends received directly by non-residents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I gave some warning in the budget speech a year ago of the steps that might have to be taken if there was not some indication forthcoming of less proliferation of small corporations with a view to taking broad advantage of the provision for lower taxation on corporations on the first $25,000 of corporate income. Notwithstanding the warning we found that this proliferation has continued and accordingly the only way in which the situation can adequately be met is to change the rules for determining what are for this purpose associated companies.
In recent years the law has provided that only one of a group of associated companies may qualify for the lower rate on the first $25,000. The rule for determining if companies are associated has been based on the ownership of 70 per cent or more of the

issued common shares of the companies concerned. When I spoke on this subject last year I indicated that an amendment might be necessary to revise the rules for determining when companies shall be deemed to be associated. I indicated that it was becoming too easy to divide a corporation into a number of smaller components each of which may qualify for the low rate of tax on its first $25,000 of income. I also indicated that consideration was being given to the possible necessity of introducing some appropriate measure to deal with this method of tax avoidance.
The amendment here proposed will necessarily be technical and I think can best be studied when we have the provisions of the bill before us. Briefly it will replace the 70 per cent ownership rule with a rule related to control of the corporation. This change is necessary because it has been found that companies can be split up under the 70 per cent ownership rule in such a way that control of the new companies and a large part of their income remains in the hands of the owners of the original company. Also the reference to common shares has been found to be inadequate because of the use of other kinds of shares. An effort will be made in the bill to recognize the fact that there may be bona fide arrangements under which control of a number of new companies remains in the hands of one person for a temporary period during the establishment and early financing of the new companies.
I point out, Mr. Chairman, that the proposed amendment is not to go into effect until the 1961 taxation year. This will afford all companies an opportunity to become familiar with the new legislation and to adjust their affairs accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, What now becomes 12 is numbered 13 in the original resolution. Here I have a new amendment which I should like to introduce in order to broaden the effect of this new exemption. The exemption as proposed in the resolution applied to the production or marketing of sodium chloride from halite deposits. We have had representations concerning the production of potash. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, because of the similarity of conditions under which it is produced to those under which sodium chloride from halite deposits is produced, I should like to offer the following substitute paragraph for the one formerly numbered 13 and now numbered 12, to read as follows:
12.	That for the 1960 and subsequent taxation years a corporation whose principal business is production or marketing of sodium chloride or potash or whose business includes the manufacturing of products which involves processing sodium chloride or potash may deduct in computing its income drilling and exploration expenses incurred by it in the year in exploring or drilling for halite or sylvite.
I would ask my colleague the Minister of National Defence to move the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I so move.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Most of the committee will welcome the amendment as proposed by the minister. I was going to make a proposal along those lines and question why potash mining had not been taken care of. I do not think the minister has gone far enough yet. I was going to raise another question. Perhaps it can be considered in the drafting of the bill. I note that the words in the resolution restrict this form of deduction by the words "in the year". I would point out to the minister that I do not think the entitlement for deduction for drilling and exploration expenses in the mining and in the petroleum industry is restricted to within the year. I was wondering why there is a difference in the

phraseology with respect to the deduction for this mining as opposed to the present provisions for drilling and exploration expenses in ordinary metal mining and in the petroleum industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: This question of the hon. member brings out clearly certain differences between the normal operations of companies engaged in mining and those engaged in the production of sodium chloride from halite deposits and those engaged in the production of potash from sylvite. Here production results from the drilling operations virtually in the same year, I think in probably every case, and it was not thought that there was any occasion for carrying over a period of years, as in the case of ordinary mining, the drilling and exploration expenses. The two cases are not in this regard strictly comparable. I think that corporations that come within the scope of this new proposed exemption will consider themselves to have acquired under this provision an exemption or benefit of some proportion.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Have the corporations in this line of business indicated any dissatisfaction with the wording since it was announced on budget night?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: The wording of this amendment to include the extraction of potash from sylvite has not been previously announced; but as to those engaged in the extraction of sodium chloride from halite deposits, the intimations we have received are of warm approval on the part of corporations that would derive benefit from this resolution.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
On a question of amendments, except for this one, the minister has adopted a new practice-I think it is a new practice this year; I do not know whether he followed it last year or not-with respect to amendments. When he reached a decision with respect to a reasonable number of changes from his budget proposals he announced to the house his intention to put those amendments in Votes and Proceedings. I think perhaps that new step has a fair amount of merit in it. It is easier at least for those of us who are concerned with the amendments to see them as early in advance of debate on the resolution stage as we can. There is also at times an additional interlude for consideration of the amended proposals by the public. What is the administrative practice in dealing with the tax changes? Do the tax collectors deal with the minister's amendments which are included in Votes and Proceedings in the same way as they deal with the proposals in the budget resolutions

on budget night in so far as the effective date of application is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
First, may I express appreciation of the hon. gentleman's comment on the practice with respect to amendments which I inaugurated, I think two years ago-certainly I employed it last year-of giving as far in advance as possible the text of any amendments that we propose to introduce with respect to any of the budget resolutions and placing those in Votes and Proceedings of the house.
In the present case these were placed in Votes and Proceedings for Friday, May 6. The amendment now under discussion is one that has arisen subsequently as a result of further representations and further study of the proposed extension of the new provision. The hon. member has raised specifically a question as to the effective date of amendments. This gives rise to very little difficulty in relation to amendments of the Income Tax Act. It could give rise to questions in regard to the taxes on commodities-

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I was thinking more of excise taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: -where the practice has been to make the changes in taxes effective as from the night that the budget is introduced. This again is a matter of the legislation to follow. The legislation can select the date of amendment or the date of the budget. I think it will be found that in the cases here it is proposed that the amendment as well as the original resolution be made effective as from budget night. This is particularly sought by those concerned where the effect of the resolution is to relieve.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Yes. I do not think the minister will mind my diverting by way of example to the commodity type of taxation because it is perhaps more relevant from the point of view of its immediate application if it is to be applied immediately. The minister is aware that after budget night the Department of National Revenue sends to all its officials across the country an indication of the minister's proposals. If the minister has indicated in the paragraph of a resolution that the effective date is to be budget night, the officials across the country are given that advice and as soon as they receive the document with this intimation they start to carry out the law as if it had already been passed in a statute. I am wondering with respect to the next stage, amendments by way of an appendix to Votes and Proceedings, whether the same practice is followed by the revenue department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Yes, it is.

speechtext:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act to provide:
1.	That the sales tax on electric heating equipment, designed for use on a system using 230 volts or greater, for permanent installation as part of an electric heating system for buildings, be repealed, but not including electric wiring or other materials leading to or connecting such equipment to the electric power supply.
2.	That ducts for warm air systems for heating buildings, but not including materials used in their manufacture, be exempt from sales tax.
3.	That the sales tax on laryngeal speaking aids and parts therefor, including batteries specifically designed for use therewith, be repealed.
4.	That the sales tax on prepared surgical sutures be repealed.
5.	That the sales tax on goods enumerated in Customs Tariff Item 692a, that is, "articles presented from abroad in recognition of the saving of human life", be repealed.
6.	That the sales tax on perlite be repealed.
7.	That portrait photographs of individuals be exempt from sales tax.
8.	That the exemption from sales tax for,
"perforated bituminized fibre pipe for drainage
purposes not exceeding four inches in inside diameter'1
be changed to read
"perforated pipe for drainage purposes not exceeding four inches in inside diameter".
9.	That the exemption from sales tax for feeds and feed supplements be extended to include feed supplements for addition to feeds for fur-bearing animals, and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture thereof.
10.	That hardware for doors and sash not specifically mentioned in Schedule III be excluded from the sales tax exemption for articles and materials to be used in the manufacture of building materials.
11.	That the exemption from sales tax for.
"septic tanks"
be changed to read,
"septic tanks and grease traps therefor".
12.	That the exemption from sales tax for.
"Usual coverings to be used exclusively for
covering goods not subject to the consumption or sales tax and materials to be used exclusively in the manufacture of such coverings" be changed to read,
"Usual coverings or containers to be used exclusively for covering or containing goods not subject to the consumption or sales tax and to be delivered

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Excise Tax Act
and sold with the goods, and materials to he used exclusively in the manufacture of such coverings or containers".
13.	That the exemption from sales tax for,
"Materials for use only in the construction,
equipment and repair of ships over ten tons net register tonnage" be changed to read,
"Materials for use only in the equipment and repair of ships over ten tons net register tonnage".
14.	That the security required under the Excise Tax Act include bonds or other securities of or guaranteed by the Government of Canada.
15.	That any enactment founded upon this resolution be deemed to have come into force on the 1st day of April 1960.
